questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12's corrin ring holds a central cobalt ion, which gives cobalamin its name.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “In Cobalamin (Vit B12), the corrin ring is bound to this trace element”, the defining choice is “Cobalt”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Hb M, the proximal histidine in B chain is replaced by:
questions.explanation: Answer is D, as B-thalassemia minor involves one defective B gene, leading to increased HbA2 and often HbF. A, Defective mutation of one of two B genes of hemoglobin - TRUE but incomplete. B, Increased HbA2 - TRUE but incomplete. C, Increased HbF - TRUE but incomplete
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In Hb M, the proximal histidine in B chain is replaced by”, the defining choice is “Valine.”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In pregnancy & lactation, the daily dietary requirement of folic acid is:
questions.explanation: During pregnancy and lactation, folic acid requirements roughly double to about 800 micrograms/day (compared to about 400 micrograms/day for non-pregnant adults) to support increased cell division and prevent neural tube defects.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In pregnancy & lactation, the daily dietary requirement of folic acid is”, the defining choice is “800 micrograms”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Methotrexate inhibits which of the following?
options: Folic acid synthesis by human cells
questions.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking the activation (reduction) of folate to its active tetrahydrofolate form; humans don't synthesize folate de novo, and dihydropteroate synthetase inhibition describes sulfonamides' bacterial target, not methotrexate's.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Methotrexate inhibits which of the following”, the defining choice is “Folic acid activation”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Methylcobalamin is the coenzyme used for conversion of:
questions.explanation: Methylcobalamin is the coenzyme for methionine synthase, which simultaneously converts homocysteine to methionine while regenerating tetrahydrofolate from methyltetrahydrofolate - one coupled reaction described by both statements a and b.
questions.keyConcept: Romaña sign (unilateral periorbital swelling) marks acute-stage Chagas disease specifically, before chronic organ involvement develops.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Neural tube defect in fetus could be prevented by supplementation of pregnant female with:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is a well-known cause of drug-induced aplastic anemia (via bone marrow toxicity), not a treatment for it; actual treatments include corticosteroids, erythropoietin, anabolic steroids, and cyclosporine.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol causes aplastic anemia rather than treating it, unlike corticosteroids, erythropoietin, or cyclosporine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: PABA analogs inhibit dihydropteroate synthetase.
questions.explanation: Sulfonamide drugs are structural analogs of PABA that competitively inhibit bacterial dihydropteroate synthetase, blocking folate synthesis in bacteria (a pathway absent in humans, giving selective antibacterial toxicity).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “PABA analogs inhibit dihydropteroate synthetase.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disorder that results in the deficiency of cobalamin. In pernicious anemia, the auto-antibodies are generated against______
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia results from autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells and/or antibodies against intrinsic factor, preventing B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disorder that results in the deficiency of cobalamin. In pernicious anemia, the auto-antibodies are generated against______”, the defining choice is “Intrinsic Factor”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The adult dietary requirement of cobalamin is _______
questions.explanation: The recommended daily intake of vitamin B12 for adults is approximately 2.4 micrograms/day, much lower than folate requirements.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “The adult dietary requirement of cobalamin is _______”, the defining choice is “2.4 microgram/day”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following drugs inhibit folate reductase enzyme in human?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits human (and bacterial/parasitic) dihydrofolate reductase; trimethoprim selectively inhibits the bacterial enzyme with much lower affinity for the human enzyme, making it a safer antibacterial.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following drugs inhibit folate reductase enzyme in human”, the defining choice is “Methotrexate”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best timing of folic acid supplementation in pregnancy?
options: Starting from the end of second trimester
When plasma folate concentration falls down
When erythrocyte folate concentration is low
questions.explanation: Because neural tube closure occurs very early (within the first 4 weeks of gestation, often before pregnancy is even recognized), folic acid supplementation is recommended to begin before conception (pre-conception), not after deficiency develops or later in pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following is the best timing of folic acid supplementation in pregnancy”, the defining choice is “Starting before pregnancy”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the characteristic feature of anemia caused by the folic acid deficiency?
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, producing large, immature red cell precursors characteristic of megaloblastic anemia (as does B12 deficiency), rather than microcytic or hypochromic anemia (seen in iron deficiency).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following is the characteristic feature of anemia caused by the folic acid deficiency”, the defining choice is “Megaloblastic anemia”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the specific transport protein for cobalamin?
questions.explanation: Transcobalamin (specifically transcobalamin II) is the plasma transport protein that carries absorbed vitamin B12 to tissues; intrinsic factor is needed for intestinal absorption, not blood transport, and transferrin transports iron, not B12.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Which of the following is the specific transport protein for cobalamin”, the defining choice is “Transcobalamin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following organ serves as storage for cobalamin?
questions.explanation: The liver is the major storage site for vitamin B12, holding several years' worth of reserves, which is why B12 deficiency symptoms develop slowly.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following organ serves as storage for cobalamin”, the defining choice is “Liver”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency may lead to megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency (like folate deficiency) impairs DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors, producing megaloblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which vitamin deficiency may lead to megaloblastic anemia”, the defining choice is “Vitamin B12”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A free radical has:
options: the ability to attack sound molecules
questions.explanation: A free radical is defined by having an unpaired electron, and this instability is precisely what drives it to react aggressively with and damage otherwise stable ('sound') molecules - both properties describe the same entity.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “A free radical has”, the defining choice is “both (A) and (B)”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: One of the following is not an antioxidant:
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, C, and E are well-known antioxidants, whereas vitamin K functions in gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors and has no antioxidant role.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “One of the following is not an antioxidant”, the defining choice is “Vitamin K”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Premature infants are not to be exposed to high-oxygen atmosphere because they have:
options: high lipid peroxides levels to produce superoxide dismutase not fully developed
high uric acid in their plasma
low ventilation capacity of their lungs
the capacity to produce superoxide dismutase not fully developed
questions.explanation: Premature infants have immature antioxidant enzyme systems, especially superoxide dismutase, so high-oxygen exposure generates reactive oxygen species that cannot be adequately neutralized, contributing to conditions like retinopathy of prematurity.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Premature infants are not to be exposed to high-oxygen atmosphere because they have”, the defining choice is “the capacity to produce superoxide dismutase not fully developed”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Selenium is needed for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Selenium is an essential cofactor of glutathione peroxidase, the antioxidant enzyme that reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides using glutathione.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Selenium is needed for which of the following”, the defining choice is “Glutathione peroxidase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The free radical-initiated and propagated-chain reaction is called lipid peroxidation because:
options: unsaturated lipids are the most susceptible molecules
questions.explanation: Polyunsaturated fatty acids, with their multiple double bonds, are especially vulnerable to free-radical attack, making them the most susceptible target of the chain reaction called lipid peroxidation.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “The free radical-initiated and propagated-chain reaction is called lipid peroxidation because”, the defining choice is “unsaturated lipids are the most susceptible molecules”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: To increase the antioxidant power, one may take any of the following except:
questions.explanation: Iron is a pro-oxidant, not an antioxidant - free iron catalyzes the Fenton reaction, generating damaging hydroxyl radicals, whereas vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, and selenium (a glutathione peroxidase cofactor) all support antioxidant defense.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “To increase the antioxidant power, one may take any of the following except”, the defining choice is “iron”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presented in the hospital with hemolytic attacks and bleeding. Enzymatic analysis detected pyruvate kinase enzyme deficiency. One of the following is true as regard this case:
options: Blood film RBCs showed loss of biconcave shape
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic ATP shortage in RBCs, leading to membrane cation pump failure and loss of the normal biconcave disc shape, seen on blood film; hemoglobin is low (hemolytic anemia, not normal), glycolysis fails to yield 2 ATP (net ATP = 0), and pyruvate kinase level/activity would be abnormal, not normal.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “A 2-year-old child presented in the hospital with hemolytic attacks and bleeding. Enzymatic analysis detected pyruvate kinase enzyme deficiency. One of the following is true as regard this case”, the defining choice is “Blood film RBCs showed loss of biconcave shape”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of ____ is the most common cause among these glycolytic enzymes of enzymatic hemolytic anemia
questions.explanation: Among glycolytic enzyme defects, pyruvate kinase deficiency is the most common cause of hereditary non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia, impairing ATP production needed to maintain RBC membrane integrity.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Deficiency of ____ is the most common cause among these glycolytic enzymes of enzymatic hemolytic anemia”, the defining choice is “Pyruvate kinase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Effects of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate on O2 affinity of Hemoglobin include:
options: unable hemoglobin to release O2 to tissue
bind to alpha chains of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin's beta chains and stabilizes the low-affinity T-state, thereby decreasing hemoglobin's O2 affinity and promoting O2 release to tissues.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Effects of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate on O2 affinity of Hemoglobin include”, the defining choice is “decrease O2 affinity of hemoglobin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Factors that increase absorption of iron include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Answer is B, as folic acid deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic anemia. A, Microcytic anemia - FALSE because this is caused by iron deficiency. C, Hypochromic anemia - FALSE because this is caused by iron deficiency. D, None of the above - FALSE because megaloblastic anemia is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Factors that increase absorption of iron include all of the following EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Pregnancy”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fluoride is added to blood samples for glucose estimation as it prevents glycolysis through inhibition of:
questions.explanation: Sodium fluoride inhibits enolase, halting glycolysis in collected blood samples so that glucose is not artificially degraded before laboratory measurement.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Fluoride is added to blood samples for glucose estimation as it prevents glycolysis through inhibition of”, the defining choice is “Enolase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: For each glucose molecule metabolized in the aerobic glycolytic pathway, there is a net production of:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis itself, regardless of downstream aerobic or anaerobic fate of pyruvate, has a net yield of 2 ATP per glucose molecule (4 ATP produced minus 2 ATP invested).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “For each glucose molecule metabolized in the aerobic glycolytic pathway, there is a net production of”, the defining choice is “2 ATP”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fructose 2,6 bis phosphate activates:
questions.explanation: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), promoting glycolysis, especially in liver under the fed state.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Fructose 2,6 bis phosphate activates”, the defining choice is “Phosphofructokinase I”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycolysis in liver cells can be inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Citrate is an allosteric inhibitor of phosphofructokinase-1, slowing glycolysis when downstream biosynthetic precursors are abundant; insulin, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, and AMP all promote (not inhibit) glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Glycolysis in liver cells can be inhibited by”, the defining choice is “Citrate”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycolysis occurs in:
questions.explanation: All ten reactions of glycolysis take place in the cytosol, which is why anucleate, mitochondria-free RBCs can still perform glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Glycolysis occurs in”, the defining choice is “Cytosol”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycolysis under anaerobic condition ends by:
questions.explanation: Under anaerobic conditions, lactate dehydrogenase converts the 2 pyruvate produced back to 2 lactate while regenerating 2 NAD+ (needed to keep glycolysis running), with a net yield of 2 ATP overall from the pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Glycolysis under anaerobic condition ends by”, the defining choice is “2 Lactic acid + 2 NAD+ + 2 ATP”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycolysis under anaerobic conditions ends by:
questions.explanation: Under anaerobic conditions, lactate dehydrogenase reduces the 2 pyruvate to 2 lactate while regenerating 2 NAD+ from the 2 NADH produced earlier, allowing glycolysis to continue.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Glycolysis under anaerobic conditions ends by”, the defining choice is “2 Lactic acid + 2 NAD+”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hepcidin is produced in ____
questions.explanation: Answer is D, as 65-75% of body iron is in hemoglobin within red blood cells. A, Iron bound to transferrin - FALSE because this is ~0.1% of total iron. B, Iron stored in the liver - FALSE because storage accounts for 15-20%. C, Myoglobin - FALSE because it accounts for ~ 4%.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Hepcidin is produced in ____”, the defining choice is “RBC.”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hexokinase is inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Hexokinase is allosterically inhibited by its own product, glucose 6-phosphate, in classic feedback inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Hexokinase is inhibited by”, the defining choice is “glucose 6-P”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How many net ATP are produced in a case of genetic absence of pyruvate kinase in RBCs?
questions.explanation: Malarial (hemozoin) pigment is a byproduct of the parasite's digestion of hemoglobin, formed and retained inside the parasite itself, which resides inside the infected RBC -- so the pigment is located inside the RBC and inside the parasite.
questions.keyConcept: Hemozoin (malarial pigment) forms inside the parasite, which itself resides inside the infected RBC.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In 2,3 BPG shunt in RBCs 1 ATP is lost as 2,3 BPG dissociates to 3 PG and Pi without generation of ATP.
questions.explanation: Because the shunt bypasses the ATP-generating phosphoglycerate kinase step, and 2,3-BPG is later dephosphorylated to 3-phosphoglycerate without producing ATP, one ATP that would normally be generated in glycolysis is effectively lost.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In 2,3 BPG shunt in RBCs 1 ATP is lost as 2,3 BPG dissociates to 3 PG and Pi without generation of ATP.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In 2,3 BPG shunt which of the following enzymes is bypassed?
questions.explanation: The Rapoport-Luebering (2,3-BPG) shunt bypasses phosphoglycerate kinase, diverting 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG instead of directly generating ATP at that step.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In 2,3 BPG shunt which of the following enzymes is bypassed”, the defining choice is “phosphoglycerate Kinase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Irreversible steps of Glycolysis are catalyzed by:
options: Glucokinase, Pyruvate Kinase, Glyceraldehyde 3 Phosphate Dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: The three committed, physiologically irreversible steps of glycolysis are catalyzed by hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1, and pyruvate kinase - the pathway's key regulatory enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Irreversible steps of Glycolysis are catalyzed by”, the defining choice is “Hexokinase, Phosphofructokinase-1, Pyruvate Kinase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: One of the following is a Substrate level phosphorylation reaction in glycolysis:
questions.explanation: Phosphoglycerate kinase directly transfers a phosphate group from 1,3-BPG to ADP, forming ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; succinate thiokinase is a TCA-cycle (not glycolytic) substrate-level phosphorylation enzyme, and hexokinase/glucokinase/PFK-1 consume rather than generate ATP.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “One of the following is a Substrate level phosphorylation reaction in glycolysis”, the defining choice is “Phosphoglycerate kinase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Pyruvate kinase is stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, the product of the PFK-1 reaction upstream, allosterically activates pyruvate kinase in a feed-forward activation loop that keeps glycolysis flowing efficiently.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Pyruvate kinase is stimulated by”, the defining choice is “fructose 1,6 bis P”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: RBCs Can produce energy by which of the following pathway
questions.explanation: Since mature RBCs lack mitochondria, they rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis (converting glucose to lactate) to generate ATP; they cannot perform gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, or fatty acid oxidation/synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “RBCs Can produce energy by which of the following pathway”, the defining choice is “Glycolysis”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The average daily iron requirement
questions.explanation: Answer is B, as transferrin is the plasma glycoprotein that transports iron in the blood. A, Ferroprotein - FALSE because this is not a specific transport protein. C, DMT - FALSE because divalent metal transporter (DMT-1) transports iron into intestinal cells. D, Ceruloplasmin - FALSE because it is a copper-containing enzyme with ferroxidase activity.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “The average daily iron requirement”, the defining choice is “3-6 mg/day”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The end product of glycolysis in RBCs is _____ ATP.
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis yields a net of 2 ATP per glucose molecule, which is the sole energy source for mature red blood cells.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “The end product of glycolysis in RBCs is _____ ATP.”, the defining choice is “2”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The net ATP gain in pyruvate kinase deficiency is:
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the last ATP-generating step of glycolysis; its absence prevents the pathway from completing, resulting in zero net ATP production from glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “The net ATP gain in pyruvate kinase deficiency is”, the defining choice is “0”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The number of ATPs produced net by glycolysis in RBC is ____
questions.explanation: Since mature RBCs depend entirely on anaerobic glycolysis, the net ATP yield per glucose molecule is 2, which is their sole source of cellular energy.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “The number of ATPs produced net by glycolysis in RBC is ____”, the defining choice is “2”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate limiting enzyme for glycolysis is:
questions.explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) catalyzes the rate-limiting, key regulatory step of glycolysis, controlled by ATP, citrate, and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “The rate limiting enzyme for glycolysis is”, the defining choice is “Phosphofructokinase-1”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True statement about glycolysis is:
options: 3 ATPs are used in the anaerobic pathway
questions.explanation: Glycolysis converts the 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate (or lactate) molecules; it occurs in the cytosol (not mitochondria), does not completely oxidize glucose to CO2/H2O, and invests 2 (not 3) ATP in its early steps.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “True statement about glycolysis is”, the defining choice is “Conversion of glucose to 3-carbon units”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the fate of NADH produced during glycolysis?
options: Acting as a substrate for ATP synthase
questions.explanation: Cytosolic NADH generated by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase must be re-oxidized to NAD+ (via the malate-aspartate/glycerol-phosphate shuttle aerobically, or via lactate dehydrogenase anaerobically) to sustain glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “What is the fate of NADH produced during glycolysis”, the defining choice is “Oxidation to NAD+”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about functions of transferrin?
options: It can carry two ferric ions
It can deliver iron from intestine to
It can deliver iron from liver to erythroblasts
It can deliver iron to kidneys for excretion
questions.explanation: Answer is D, as the body absorbs iron in the Fe2* form and as intact heme iron from animal sources. A, Ferrous form - TRUE because Fe2* is absorbed better than Fe3* by intestinal cells. B, Ferric form - FALSE because Fe'* must be reduced to Fe2* for efficient absorption. C, Heme iron form - TRUE because heme iron is absorbed intact via a heme carrier protein.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Which of the following is true about functions of transferrin”, the defining choice is “It can deliver iron from liver to erythroblasts”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A person on ingestion of Primaquine develops hemolytic anemia, what is the possible defect?
questions.explanation: Primaquine is an oxidant drug that precipitates hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency, since their RBCs cannot generate enough NADPH to neutralize the resulting oxidative stress.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “A person on ingestion of Primaquine develops hemolytic anemia, what is the possible defect”, the defining choice is “Glucose-6-P dehydrogenase deficiency”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: By the glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction, glucose is oxidized at carbon:
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes carbon 1 of glucose-6-phosphate to form 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone while reducing NADP+ to NADPH. This is the first and rate-limiting reaction of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “By the glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction, glucose is oxidized at carbon”, the defining choice is “1”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cases of G6PD deficiency are managed by:
questions.explanation: In man, Plasmodium undergoes two asexual cycles: the exo-erythrocytic (hepatic) schizogony in liver cells after sporozoite invasion, and the erythrocytic schizogony in red blood cells. Gametocytes form in the blood but only complete their sexual cycle in the mosquito, so man is not a site of sexual reproduction.
questions.keyConcept: Man hosts two asexual cycles of Plasmodium (hepatic and erythrocytic schizogony); the sexual cycle occurs only in the mosquito.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Effects of 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate on O, affinity of Hemoglobin include:
options: Unable hemoglobin to release O, to tissue
Bind to alpha chains of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Answer is B, as 2,3-BPG decreases hemoglobin's oxygen affinity to promote release. A, Increase O2 affinity of hemoglobin - FALSE because it decreases affinity. C, Unable hemoglobin to release O, to tissue - FALSE because it facilitates release. D, Bind to alpha chains of hemoglobin - FALSE because 2,3-BPG binds beta chains
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Effects of 2,3- bisphosphoglycerate on O, affinity of Hemoglobin include”, the defining choice is “Decrease O, affinity of hemoglobin.”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Favism is ___ in inheritance.
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency (and thus favism) is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, explaining its higher prevalence and severity in males.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Favism is ___ in inheritance.”, the defining choice is “X linked”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Favism is due to_____ deficiency.
questions.explanation: Favism, an acute hemolytic reaction to fava beans, occurs in individuals with G6PD deficiency, whose RBCs cannot generate enough NADPH to counter the oxidative stress from compounds in fava beans.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Favism is due to_____ deficiency.”, the defining choice is “glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: G6PD is regulated by the amount of NADPH in the cell. What is the most plausible mechanism of regulation?
questions.explanation: G6PD activity is regulated by classic product feedback inhibition - accumulated NADPH allosterically inhibits the enzyme, matching NADPH production to cellular demand.
questions.keyConcept: Ferrous (not ferric) iron is the form absorbed most readily during oral iron therapy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycolysis proceeds only anaerobically | in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis in RBCs 7 Answer is D, as red blood cells lack mitochondria and rely on anaerobic glycolysis for energy. A, Resting muscle cells - FALSE because resting muscle uses oxidative phosphorylation. B, Liver cells - FALSE because liver cells use oxidative phosphorylation. C, Nerve cells - FALSE because nerve cells rely on oxidative phosphorylation. E, Heart cells - FALSE because heart muscle is highly aerobic and oxidizes lactate.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Glycolysis proceeds only anaerobically | in which of the following”, the defining choice is “Red blood cells.”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: HMP pathway produces which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ring forms with double (paired) chromatin dots are a classic morphological feature of Plasmodium falciparum, which also frequently shows multiple rings per infected red cell and appliqué (marginal) forms -- helping distinguish it from P. vivax/ovale (usually single chromatin dot, one ring per cell) and from Babesia (which lacks true ring-and-chromatin morphology and often shows tetrad 'Maltese cross' forms).
questions.keyConcept: Double chromatin dots and multiple rings per RBC are classic diagnostic features distinguishing P. falciparum on a blood film.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: HMP shunt is of great importance in cellular metabolism because it produces:
questions.explanation: The HMP (pentose phosphate) pathway's key products are NADPH, for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense, and ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis; it does not generate ATP.
questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback; for “HMP shunt is of great importance in cellular metabolism because it produces”, the defining choice is “NADPH”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heinz body is characteristic to _____
questions.explanation: Heinz bodies (denatured, precipitated hemoglobin aggregates) are characteristically seen in G6PD deficiency/favism, where oxidative damage to hemoglobin occurs due to insufficient NADPH-dependent antioxidant defense.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Heinz body is characteristic to _____”, the defining choice is “favism”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hexose Mono Phosphate pathway oxidizes which of the following?
questions.explanation: The oxidative phase of the HMP shunt begins with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizing glucose 6-phosphate, generating NADPH (a product, not a substrate being oxidized) and ribulose-5-phosphate.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Hexose Mono Phosphate pathway oxidizes which of the following”, the defining choice is “Glucose 6-P”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, the major products are:
questions.explanation: The oxidative branch of the HMP pathway produces ribulose 5-phosphate and NADPH (not NADH), the latter being crucial for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “In the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, the major products are”, the defining choice is “Ribulose-P and NADPH”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Insulin Induces G6PD in the well-fed state.
questions.explanation: In the well-fed state, insulin promotes induction of G6PD gene expression, boosting NADPH production to support lipogenesis and other anabolic pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Insulin Induces G6PD in the well-fed state.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Oxidation of 3 molecules of glucose by pentose phosphate pathway results in the production of:
options: 3 molecules of pentose, 6 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of CO2
4 molecules of pentose, 6 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of CO2
4 molecules of pentose, 3 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of CO2
3 molecules of pentose, 4 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of CO2
questions.explanation: Each glucose 6-phosphate oxidized through the oxidative PPP yields 2 NADPH, 1 CO2, and 1 pentose (ribulose 5-phosphate); for 3 molecules of glucose, this scales to 6 NADPH, 3 CO2, and 3 pentose molecules.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Oxidation of 3 molecules of glucose by pentose phosphate pathway results in the production of”, the defining choice is “3 molecules of pentose, 6 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of CO2”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Respiratory burst is the pathway characterized by increased O2 consumption by:
questions.explanation: The respiratory burst is the rapid production of reactive oxygen species by NADPH oxidase in activated phagocytes (neutrophils/macrophages) to kill ingested microbes.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “Respiratory burst is the pathway characterized by increased O2 consumption by”, the defining choice is “Phagocytes”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The net ATP gain in pyruvate kinase defciency is:
questions.explanation: Answer is A, as pyruvate kinase deficiency results in zero net ATP (2 consumed, 2 produced). B, 2 - FALSE because this is normal glycolysis. C, 4 - FALSE because this is gross ATP in normal glycolysis. D, 6 - FALSE because this is incorrect
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “The net ATP gain in pyruvate kinase defciency is”, the defining choice is “Zero c.”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate limiting enzyme of HMP pathway is:
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the HMP (pentose phosphate) pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “The rate limiting enzyme of HMP pathway is”, the defining choice is “glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The reverse of non-oxidative phase occurs in muscles which cannot utilize NADPH & lack G6PD.
questions.explanation: Muscle tissue has little G6PD activity and limited NADPH demand, so it runs the non-oxidative phase in reverse, converting pentoses from dietary/other sources into glycolytic intermediates rather than generating NADPH.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “The reverse of non-oxidative phase occurs in muscles which cannot utilize NADPH & lack G6PD.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What enzyme catalyses the rate limiting step of the HMP?
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the first, rate-limiting reaction of the HMP pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “What enzyme catalyses the rate limiting step of the HMP”, the defining choice is “glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the first reaction of the pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explanation: The pathway begins with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizing glucose 6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone, generating the first NADPH.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “What is the first reaction of the pentose phosphate pathway”, the defining choice is “Oxidation of glucose 6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the importance of the HMP pathway in RBCs?
options: Producing pentose for nucleic acid synthesis
questions.explanation: In the mosquito, Plasmodium undergoes a single sexual cycle (sporogony): gametocytes taken up in a blood meal fuse to form a zygote, which develops into an oocyst producing sporozoites. There is no asexual multiplication in the mosquito -- that occurs only in the human host (exo-erythrocytic and erythrocytic schizogony).
questions.keyConcept: The mosquito hosts only the sexual cycle (sporogony) of Plasmodium; all asexual multiplication occurs in humans.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where does the pentose phosphate pathway take place?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is a glycoprotein hormone that must be administered parenterally (IV or subcutaneously) because, like other protein/peptide drugs, it would be digested if taken orally; it is used to stimulate erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion needs, especially in chronic renal failure.
questions.keyConcept: Erythropoietin cannot be given orally because it is a protein hormone that would be digested in the gut.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the oxidative phase of the HMP pathway?
questions.explanation: All erythrocytic stages of P. falciparum (rings, trophozoites, schizonts, gametocytes) are NOT normally seen together in peripheral blood, since mature trophozoites and schizonts sequester in deep capillaries of internal organs -- only ring stages and crescent-shaped gametocytes typically circulate peripherally. The other statements (crescent gametocytes, irregular fever, rupture of both infected and bystander RBCs) are all true of P. falciparum.
questions.keyConcept: In P. falciparum, mature trophozoites/schizonts sequester in deep vessels, so not all blood stages appear in peripheral films.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is important for erythrocytes?
questions.explanation: Since mature RBCs lack mitochondria and rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis, lactate dehydrogenase (which regenerates NAD+ by converting pyruvate to lactate) is essential; RBCs lack glucose-6-phosphatase, glycogen stores, fatty acid synthesis, and mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following enzymes is important for erythrocytes”, the defining choice is “Lactate dehydrogenase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the use of the pentose phosphate pathway in red blood cells is correct?
options: Mature red blood cells do not need the pentose phosphate pathway since they do not divide
Mature red blood cells need the pathway to oxidize the glucose-6-phosphate
Mature red blood cells need the pathway since RBCs don't synthesize fat
Mature red blood cells need the pathway for the production of NADPH
questions.explanation: Even though mature RBCs neither divide nor synthesize fat (so they don't need ribose-5-P or NADPH for those purposes), they critically depend on the pathway for NADPH production, which maintains reduced glutathione and protects the cell from oxidative damage.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which of the following statements about the use of the pentose phosphate pathway in red blood cells is correct”, the defining choice is “Mature red blood cells need the pathway for the production of NADPH”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about oxidative pentose phosphate pathway?
options: The pathway supplies ribose 5-phosphate and NADPH in the quantities the cell requires
Glucose 6-phosphatase catalyzes the rate limiting reaction of the pathway
questions.explanation: The oxidative and non-oxidative branches of the PPP are flexibly interconverted so that the cell can generate ribose 5-phosphate and NADPH in whatever relative amounts are needed; it generates NADPH (not NADH), does not oxidize NADPH, and its rate-limiting enzyme is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, not glucose-6-phosphatase.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which of the following statements is correct about oxidative pentose phosphate pathway”, the defining choice is “The pathway supplies ribose 5-phosphate and NADPH in the quantities the cell requires”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about the non-oxidative phase pentose phosphate pathway?
options: Pentoses can converted to glycolytic intermediates
questions.explanation: The non-oxidative phase is reversible and allows pentoses (like ribulose 5-phosphate) to be converted back into glycolytic intermediates (fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate) when NADPH demand is high but ribose is not needed; transketolase (not transaldolase) requires thiamine pyrophosphate and transfers 2-carbon (not 3-carbon) units.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which of the following statements is correct about the non-oxidative phase pentose phosphate pathway”, the defining choice is “Pentoses can converted to glycolytic intermediates”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct about the pentose phosphate pathway?
options: It not used for ATP synthesis
It generates 38 mol of ATP per mole of glucose consumed
It is a reductive pathway that consumes NADH
Present in plants but not in animals
questions.explanation: Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm arising from a JAK2-mutated hematopoietic stem cell, causing excessive proliferation of erythroid (and often myeloid/megakaryocytic) precursors independent of erythropoietin. Plummer-Vinson syndrome, thalassemia major, and subacute combined degeneration are not myeloproliferative disorders -- they reflect iron deficiency, a hemoglobinopathy, and vitamin B12 deficiency, respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Polycythemia vera is a JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm, distinct from iron-deficiency, hemoglobinopathy, or B12-deficiency conditions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one out of the following enzymes present in the pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explanation: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase catalyzes the second oxidative step of the PPP, converting 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose 5-phosphate with production of a second NADPH; the other enzymes belong to glycolysis or glycogenolysis.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which one out of the following enzymes present in the pentose phosphate pathway”, the defining choice is “6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A jaundiced patient has elevated direct bilirubin with normal levels of indirect bilirubin. This patient is probably:
options: Suffering from an obstructed gall bladder
questions.explanation: Posterior station development -- where the parasite matures in the hindgut of the vector and the infective (metacyclic) stage is passed in the insect's faeces, contaminating the bite wound or mucous membranes rather than being injected by the bite itself -- is the classic transmission pattern of Trypanosoma cruzi in the triatomine (reduviid) bug, termed 'Monomorphic trypanosoma' in this course's terminology. This contrasts with anterior station development (maturation in the salivary glands/proboscis, transmitted by the bite itself), which is how African trypanosomes (T. gambiense/rhodesiense) and Plasmodium are transmitted.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior station (hindgut) development with faecal transmission is the hallmark of T. cruzi in the triatomine bug, not African trypanosomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Among the manifestations of hemolytic jaundice are:
questions.explanation: Hemolytic jaundice increases unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin production, which the liver processes into extra bilirubin/urobilinogen that appears in increased amounts in urine; stools are typically normal or dark (not faint, which suggests biliary obstruction), so options a and b together are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Among the manifestations of hemolytic jaundice are”, the defining choice is “A and B”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Bilirubin is formed in:
questions.explanation: Bilirubin is produced mainly in the reticuloendothelial system, particularly the spleen and bone marrow, where senescent red blood cells are broken down and heme is catabolized.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Bilirubin is formed in”, the defining choice is “Spleen & bone marrow”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Concerning heme catabolism, the following are true, EXCEPT:
options: The heme ring is split at the alpha-methene bridge to form biliverdin
Bilirubin is transported to the liver carried on albumin
Bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid in the liver
questions.explanation: Biliverdin is reduced BY biliverdin reductase TO bilirubin, not the reverse; heme is first split at the alpha-methene bridge (via heme oxygenase, releasing CO) to form biliverdin, which is then reduced to bilirubin, transported on albumin to the liver, and conjugated with glucuronic acid there.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Concerning heme catabolism, the following are true, EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Reduction of bilirubin produces biliverdin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Concerning neonatal jaundice, all are correct, EXCEPT:
options: It results from accelerated hemolysis and/or immature hepatic system
There is high plasma level of conjugated bilirubin
If bilirubin level exceeds 20 mg/dL, it may lead to kernicterus
It is treated by phenobarbital and phototherapy
If it is not treated it leads to mental retardation
questions.explanation: True relapse (recurrence of clinical malaria after apparent cure of the blood infection) occurs in P. vivax and P. ovale because they form dormant liver-stage hypnozoites that can reactivate weeks to years later; P. falciparum and P. malariae lack hypnozoites and instead cause recrudescence (from persisting blood-stage parasites) rather than true relapse.
questions.keyConcept: True relapse from dormant hepatic hypnozoites is unique to P. vivax and P. ovale among the malaria parasites.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia can be caused by each of the following conditions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Glucuronyl transferase deficiency (as in Gilbert or Crigler-Najjar syndromes) impairs bilirubin conjugation and causes unconjugated (not conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia; bile duct obstruction, gallstones, and Dubin-Johnson syndrome (impaired excretion of already-conjugated bilirubin) all cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia can be caused by each of the following conditions EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Glucuronyl transferase deficiency”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Manifest jaundice occurs when plasma bilirubin level exceeds:
questions.explanation: Clinically visible (manifest) jaundice appears once plasma bilirubin exceeds approximately 2-3 mg/dL, when it becomes deposited in tissues enough to be seen as yellow discoloration.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Manifest jaundice occurs when plasma bilirubin level exceeds”, the defining choice is “3 mg/dL”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Normal level of total bilirubin in plasma is less than:
questions.explanation: Normal total plasma bilirubin is typically below about 1.2 mg/dL (roughly 0.2-1.0 mg/dL in most reference ranges).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Normal level of total bilirubin in plasma is less than”, the defining choice is “1.2 mg/dL”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The color of a healing bruise goes from reddish-purple to green and finally to yellow. This color sequence is due to the conversion of:
options: Localized heme to biliverdin to bilirubin
Localized heme to urobilinogen to stercobilinogen
Bilirubin to mono-conjugated bilirubin to di-conjugated bilirubin
questions.explanation: Local heme released from extravasated blood in a bruise is oxidized by heme oxygenase to green biliverdin, which is then reduced by biliverdin reductase to yellow bilirubin, producing the characteristic reddish-purple to green to yellow color change as it heals.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “The color of a healing bruise goes from reddish-purple to green and finally to yellow. This color sequence is due to the conversion of”, the defining choice is “Localized heme to biliverdin to bilirubin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Unconjugated bilirubin:
options: Is the component measured as 'direct bilirubin'
Is more soluble in aqueous solutions than conjugated bilirubin
Is the predominant form of bilirubin found in bile
Is esterified by one or two UDP-glucuronic acids
questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin does not react directly with diazo reagents and must be measured indirectly (by subtracting direct from total bilirubin); it is water-insoluble (not more soluble than conjugated bilirubin), is not the predominant bile pigment, and is not esterified with glucuronic acid (that describes conjugated bilirubin).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Unconjugated bilirubin”, the defining choice is “Is measured 'indirectly' by diazo reagents”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Urobilinogen is formed:
questions.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin excreted into the intestine is converted to urobilinogen by intestinal bacteria; some urobilinogen is reabsorbed and later excreted in urine, but its formation occurs in the intestine.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Urobilinogen is formed”, the defining choice is “In the intestine by bacteria”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following porphyrin derivatives is conjugated, reacts directly, and is a major component of bile?
questions.explanation: Bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated bilirubin) reacts directly with diazo reagents (giving the 'direct bilirubin' measurement) and is the major bile pigment excreted into bile after conjugation in the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following porphyrin derivatives is conjugated, reacts directly, and is a major component of bile”, the defining choice is “Bilirubin diglucuronide”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: 8-Aminolevulinic acid synthase activity:
options: Given for 6 months to replenish iron stores
questions.explanation: Carbonyl iron is 100% elemental iron, given orally (usually after meals to reduce GI upset), but the typical duration to replenish iron stores after hemoglobin normalizes is about 2-3 months, not a fixed 6 months -- making the 6-month statement the incorrect one.
questions.keyConcept: Iron repletion after Hb normalization typically takes about 2-3 months, not 6 months as stated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ALA dehydratase catalyzes conversion of ALA into:
questions.explanation: ALA dehydratase (a zinc-requiring enzyme also inhibited by lead) condenses two molecules of ALA into porphobilinogen (PBG), the pyrrole ring precursor of heme.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “ALA dehydratase catalyzes conversion of ALA into”, the defining choice is “Porphobilinogen”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ALA synthase catalyzes condensation of succinyl CoA with:
questions.explanation: ALA synthase condenses succinyl-CoA with glycine (not alanine, cysteine, threonine, or serine) to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), releasing CO2 and CoA.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “ALA synthase catalyzes condensation of succinyl CoA with”, the defining choice is “None of the above”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ALA synthase requires:
questions.explanation: ALA synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, the active form of vitamin B6) as its essential coenzyme to condense glycine with succinyl-CoA.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “ALA synthase requires”, the defining choice is “PLP”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Biosynthesis of Heme occur in all tissues especially RBCs.
questions.explanation: The combination of fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and dysentery-like gastrointestinal symptoms is characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis (kala azar), reflecting reticuloendothelial (spleen, liver, marrow) and intestinal mucosal involvement by Leishmania donovani amastigotes -- distinguishing it from T. cruzi, Toxoplasma, W. bancrofti, and African trypanosomiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and dysentery together point to visceral leishmaniasis (kala azar).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase leads to:
questions.explanation: Impaired ALA synthase activity (as in X-linked sideroblastic anemia or B6 deficiency) blocks the first step of heme synthesis, leading to iron-loaded, ring sideroblasts in bone marrow - the hallmark of sideroblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Deficiency of delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase leads to”, the defining choice is “Sideroblastic anemia”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of uroporphyrinogen I synthase leads to:
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen I synthase (also called PBG deaminase/hydroxymethylbilane synthase) deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, characterized by acute neuropsychiatric attacks without photosensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Deficiency of uroporphyrinogen I synthase leads to”, the defining choice is “Acute intermittent porphyria”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which enzyme causes porphyria not associated with photosensitivity?
questions.explanation: ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria causes accumulation of ALA (and some PBG), neither of which is photosensitizing, unlike the accumulated porphyrinogens/porphyrins in enzyme defects further down the pathway (e.g., ferrochelatase or porphyrinogen oxidase deficiency), which do cause photosensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Deficiency of which enzyme causes porphyria not associated with photosensitivity”, the defining choice is “Porphyrinogen synthase (ALA dehydratase)”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which vitamin can cause sideroblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6, as its active coenzyme form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), is required by ALA synthase for heme synthesis; its deficiency impairs heme production in developing erythroblasts, producing sideroblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Deficiency of which vitamin can cause sideroblastic anemia”, the defining choice is “PLP (Vit. B6)”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which vitamin causes sideroblastic anemia?
options: Corticosteroids / decreases bleeding due to thrombocytopenia.
Cyclosporin / elevates red blood cell level
questions.explanation: Cyclosporine acts by immunosuppression in aplastic anemia rather than directly elevating red blood cell counts, making the pairing 'Cyclosporin / elevates red blood cell level' incorrect; corticosteroids reduce thrombocytopenic bleeding, antibiotics treat infection, and erythropoietin does directly stimulate RBC production.
questions.keyConcept: The mismatch is that cyclosporine's action in aplastic anemia is immunosuppressive, not a direct RBC-elevating effect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity:
options: In liver is frequently decreased in individuals treated with drugs such as the barbiturate phenobarbital
Catalyzes a rate-limiting reaction in porphyrin biosynthesis
Is strongly inhibited by heavy metal ions such as lead
questions.explanation: ALA synthase catalyzes the rate-limiting, first step of heme synthesis. Hepatic ALA synthase (ALAS1) is actually induced (increased), not decreased, by barbiturates; it requires PLP, not biotin; it occurs in mitochondria; and lead mainly inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, not ALA synthase directly.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity”, the defining choice is “Catalyzes a rate-limiting reaction in porphyrin biosynthesis”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase:
options: Can be induced by phenobarbital and some steroids
questions.explanation: ALA synthase requires PLP as coenzyme, is transcriptionally induced by drugs like phenobarbital (via cytochrome P450 induction increasing heme demand) and certain steroids, and is feedback-inhibited by heme itself (via repression of gene expression and inhibition of mitochondrial import) - all three statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme biosynthesis occurs in:
questions.explanation: Heme synthesis occurs mainly in the liver (for cytochromes) and bone marrow erythroid precursors (for hemoglobin), the two tissues with the greatest heme synthetic demand.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Heme biosynthesis occurs in”, the defining choice is “Liver and bone marrow”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme is a tetrapyrrole structure consisting of Fe2+ ions in the center of the porphyrin ring. All the following proteins contain Heme except?
questions.explanation: Chyluria (chyle/lymphatic fluid in urine) results from lymphatic obstruction and rupture of dilated lymphatics into the urinary tract, a recognized complication of chronic Wuchereria bancrofti infection, distinguishing it from T. cruzi, Toxoplasma, and kala azar, which do not cause lymphatic obstruction.
questions.keyConcept: Chyluria results from lymphatic obstruction/rupture, a recognized complication specific to chronic W. bancrofti infection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme is synthesized by condensation of:
questions.explanation: Kerandel's sign (delayed cutaneous hyperesthesia -- pain on deep palpation or light pressure, appearing after a delay) is a classic clinical feature of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) caused by Trypanosoma gambiense/rhodesiense, distinguishing it from Chagas disease, visceral leishmaniasis, and filariasis, which do not produce this sign.
questions.keyConcept: Kerandel's sign (delayed hyperesthesia) is a hallmark clinical feature specific to African trypanosomiasis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme synthesis does NOT occur in
questions.explanation: The answer is C, as the distal histidine (His E7) stabilizes oxygen but does not bind to iron. Option A, the proximal histidine, is false because it binds directly to iron. Option B, oxygen, is false because it binds to iron. Option D, the pyrrole nitrogens, is false because they also bind to iron.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Heme synthesis does NOT occur in”, the defining choice is “RBCs”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hypoxia increases activity of _____ in erythropoietic tissues.
questions.explanation: The buffy coat concentration technique (concentrating the leukocyte layer after centrifugation) can enhance detection of intracellular/blood parasites across multiple hemoflagellate infections, including African trypanosomes (both gambiense and rhodesiense), T. cruzi, and visceral Leishmania, all of which may be present in low numbers in peripheral blood.
questions.keyConcept: Buffy coat concentration is a shared diagnostic technique useful across multiple hemoflagellate infections with low-level parasitemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Bone Marrow, ALAS2 is derepressed by barbiturates.
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is the classic opportunistic protozoan: latent infection can reactivate and cause severe, life-threatening disease (encephalitis) specifically in immunocompromised patients (e.g., AIDS), unlike African trypanosomes or T. cruzi, which cause disease independent of immune status.
questions.keyConcept: Toxoplasma gondii is an opportunistic pathogen that reactivates specifically in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In heme synthesis in mammalian cells:
options: Succinyl CoA and alanine are the immediate substrates for formation of delta-aminolevulinic acid
Ferric iron is inserted into protoporphyrin IX
Porphobilinogen is formed by the condensation of two molecules of delta-aminolevulinic acid
TPP is a coenzyme for ALA synthase
questions.explanation: Porphobilinogen (PBG) is formed by ALA dehydratase condensing two molecules of ALA; the true substrates for ALA formation are succinyl-CoA and glycine (not alanine), ferrous (not ferric) iron is inserted by ferrochelatase, coproporphyrinogen III (not 'coproporphyrin IV') is the true intermediate, and ALA synthase requires PLP (vitamin B6), not TPP.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “In heme synthesis in mammalian cells”, the defining choice is “Porphobilinogen is formed by the condensation of two molecules of delta-aminolevulinic acid”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In lead poisoning, which of the followings is seen in urine?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase, so delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) accumulates and is excreted in excess in the urine, a classic diagnostic marker of lead poisoning.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “In lead poisoning, which of the followings is seen in urine”, the defining choice is “delta-ALA”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Isoniazid therapy of tuberculosis may cause vitamin B6 deficiency, which may lead to anemia due to deficient:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (as PLP) is the essential cofactor for ALA synthase, the enzyme that condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA to form ALA, the first step of heme synthesis; B6 deficiency impairs this step, causing sideroblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Isoniazid therapy of tuberculosis may cause vitamin B6 deficiency, which may lead to anemia due to deficient”, the defining choice is “Synthesis of aminolevulinic acid”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lead inhibits:
questions.explanation: Lead is a classic inhibitor of both ALA dehydratase (ALA to PBG step) and ferrochelatase (final iron-insertion step), causing accumulation of ALA and protoporphyrin and a sideroblastic-type, microcytic anemia; it does not directly inhibit ALA synthase.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Lead inhibits”, the defining choice is “A and C”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lead poisoning causes the increase in the accumulation and urinary excretion of coproporphyrin III and ALA in the urine. Which of the following enzymes are inhibited by lead metal?
questions.explanation: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) characteristically destroys autonomic ganglia in the heart and gastrointestinal tract, leading to chronic cardiomyopathy, mega-esophagus, and megacolon -- a distinctive triad not seen with African trypanosomiasis, visceral leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis, or Brugia malayi infection.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic Chagas disease's ganglion destruction produces the distinctive cardiomyopathy/mega-esophagus/megacolon triad.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lead poisoning leads to inhibition of which enzymes?
questions.explanation: In the malaria life cycle, man is the intermediate host, harboring the asexual cycle (exo-erythrocytic schizogony in the liver, then erythrocytic schizogony in RBCs); the mosquito is the definitive host, harboring the sexual cycle (sporogony) that produces infective sporozoites.
questions.keyConcept: Man is the intermediate host (asexual cycle) for Plasmodium; the mosquito is the definitive host (sexual cycle).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: One of the following intermediates is formed in the cytosol:
questions.explanation: Hydroxymethylbilane (formed by PBG deaminase acting on porphobilinogen) is a cytosolic intermediate; ALA is made in mitochondria, while protoporphyrinogen and protoporphyrin IX formation/oxidation occurs back in the mitochondria.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “One of the following intermediates is formed in the cytosol”, the defining choice is “Hydroxymethylbilane”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Persons exhibiting congenital erythropoietic porphyria have defective:
questions.explanation: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria results from deficient uroporphyrinogen III synthase (also called uroporphyrinogen III cosynthase), causing accumulation of the type I porphyrin isomers and severe photosensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Maurer's dots are diagnostic specifically for P. falciparum infection on a blood film.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Porphyrin ring consists of 4 pyrrole rings linked by:
questions.explanation: The four pyrrole rings of a porphyrin are joined together by four methenyl (=CH-) bridges to form the closed macrocyclic ring.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Porphyrin ring consists of 4 pyrrole rings linked by”, the defining choice is “Methenyl bridges”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Protoporphyria is due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from deficient ferrochelatase activity, which normally inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to complete heme synthesis; its deficiency causes protoporphyrin accumulation and photosensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Protoporphyria is due to deficiency of”, the defining choice is “Ferrochelatase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Synthesis of ALA occurs in:
questions.explanation: ALA synthase is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme, so the first step of heme synthesis (formation of ALA from glycine and succinyl-CoA) occurs in the mitochondria.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Synthesis of ALA occurs in”, the defining choice is “Mitochondria”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate limiting enzyme of Heme synthesis present in:
questions.explanation: Herbivorous animals like cattle become infected with Toxoplasma by grazing on pasture contaminated with sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces, whereas carnivores (including humans) become infected mainly by eating tissue cysts (bradyzoites) in the meat of infected herbivores -- the two infective routes correspond to the animal's diet.
questions.keyConcept: Herbivores acquire Toxoplasma via ingestion of sporulated oocysts from contaminated pasture, not tissue cysts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The sequence of heme synthesis from delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is:
options: ALA → porphobilinogen → uroporphyrinogen → protoporphyrin → protoporphyrinogen → heme
ALA → porphobilinogen → uroporphyrinogen → protoporphyrinogen → protoporphyrin → heme
ALA → uroporphyrinogen → porphobilinogen → protoporphyrinogen → protoporphyrin → heme
questions.explanation: The correct order is ALA to PBG (ALA dehydratase), PBG to uroporphyrinogen (PBG deaminase), then decarboxylation/oxidation to protoporphyrinogen, then to protoporphyrin (protoporphyrinogen oxidase), and finally ferrochelatase inserts iron to form heme.
questions.keyConcept: Schuffner's dots specifically mark RBCs infected by P. vivax or P. ovale, not P. malariae or P. falciparum.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The synthesis of heme involves both cytosolic and mitochondrial cellular compartments. Which of the following enzyme-catalyzed reaction occurs in the cytosol?
questions.explanation: The Sabin-Feldman dye test for toxoplasmosis uses live ('living') Toxoplasma organisms as antigen: patient antibody plus complement lyses the live organisms, which then fail to stain with methylene blue, distinguishing it from the Leishmanin skin test (killed antigen), the card agglutination trypanosomiasis test, and the IgG avidity test, none of which use a living-organism substrate.
questions.keyConcept: The Sabin-Feldman dye test uniquely uses live Toxoplasma organisms as its antigen substrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following Vitamin is important in Heme synthesis?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (as pyridoxal phosphate) is the essential coenzyme for ALA synthase, making it critical for heme synthesis; its deficiency (or antagonism by drugs like isoniazid) causes sideroblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which of the following Vitamin is important in Heme synthesis”, the defining choice is “Vitamin B6 Pyridoxine”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids used in Heme Synthesis?
questions.explanation: The Montenegro (leishmanin) skin test detects delayed-type hypersensitivity to Leishmania antigen and becomes positive as cellular immunity develops during recovery, making it useful as a test of cure/exposure in kala azar, whereas it is not relevant to sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, or elephantiasis.
questions.keyConcept: The Montenegro skin test reflects developing cellular immunity in kala azar, making it useful as a test of cure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes in heme synthesis requires Zn2+?
questions.explanation: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents characteristically raise blood pressure and increase thrombotic risk (by raising hematocrit/blood viscosity), not cause hypotension -- this is a recognized adverse effect requiring blood pressure monitoring during therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Erythropoietin therapy characteristically causes hypertension and thrombosis, not hypotension.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not required in the delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase reaction?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA using PLP (vitamin B6) as cofactor; iron is incorporated later by ferrochelatase, not required for this first step.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Which of the following is not required in the delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase reaction”, the defining choice is “Iron”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the rate limiting step of Heme synthesis?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme biosynthesis, condensing glycine and succinyl-CoA to form ALA.
