questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which of the following is the rate limiting step of Heme synthesis”, the defining choice is “ALA synthase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following reactions take place in cytoplasm NOT mitochondria?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is a recognized cause of aplastic anemia through bone marrow toxicity, not a treatment for it; the actual treatments for aplastic anemia include corticosteroids, erythropoietin, anabolic steroids, and cyclosporine.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol is excluded because it causes (rather than treats) aplastic anemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following reactions takes place in cytoplasm, not mitochondria?
questions.explanation: After ALA is made in mitochondria and exported, the cytosolic steps (ALA dehydratase through protoporphyrinogen formation) occur in the cytosol; the last three steps (protoporphyrinogen oxidase, and ferrochelatase inserting iron) occur back in the mitochondria.
questions.keyConcept: Maurer's clefts are the characteristic coarse stippling of P. falciparum-infected RBCs, distinct from Schuffner's dots.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements about ALA synthase is correct?
options: It catalyzes the rate-limiting reaction in heme degradation
It catalyzes the rate-limiting reaction in heme synthesis
ALA synthase is inhibited by lead
questions.explanation: ALA synthase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis (not degradation); it requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), not biotin, as its coenzyme, and lead primarily inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, not ALA synthase.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which of the following statements about ALA synthase is correct”, the defining choice is “It catalyzes the rate-limiting reaction in heme synthesis”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which out of the following catalyzes the rate limiting step in the pathway of heme biosynthesis?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme biosynthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which out of the following catalyzes the rate limiting step in the pathway of heme biosynthesis”, the defining choice is “ALA synthase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ______ is responsible for hydroxylation of xenobiotics as drugs.
questions.explanation: Chorioretinitis (inflammation of the choroid and retina) is a classic ocular manifestation of toxoplasmosis, occurring in both congenital and reactivated infections, distinguishing Toxoplasma from T. cruzi, kala azar, W. bancrofti, and African trypanosomes, which do not characteristically cause this eye finding.
questions.keyConcept: Chorioretinitis is a hallmark ocular finding of toxoplasmosis, both congenital and reactivated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: 1ry structure of myoglobin contain ______ amino acids.
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is the classic teratogenic protozoan: primary maternal infection during pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause severe congenital defects (hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification) in the fetus, unlike T. cruzi, African trypanosomes, or visceral Leishmania, which are not classically teratogenic.
questions.keyConcept: Toxoplasma gondii is the classic teratogenic protozoan causing congenital fetal malformations after transplacental transmission.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate attaches to which part of hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin, contacting positively charged residues on the two beta chains, stabilizing the low-affinity T-state.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate attaches to which part of hemoglobin”, the defining choice is “Beta chains”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A globin chain is characterized by which of the following?
options: Hydrophobic groups are generally located on the surface
The secondary structure contains 8 alpha-helices: A-H
Heme is present in a hydrophilic pocket in the center
Heme is attached by its iron to distal histidine
questions.explanation: Globin chains have a characteristic secondary structure of 8 alpha-helical segments labeled A through H; hydrophobic groups are buried internally (not on the surface), the heme pocket is hydrophobic (not hydrophilic), and heme iron binds the proximal (not distal) histidine directly.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “A globin chain is characterized by which of the following”, the defining choice is “The secondary structure contains 8 alpha-helices: A-H”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: About HbA1c, which is incorrect?
options: It is formed of four subunits
Its N-terminus β chain is conjugated with glucose
It consists of 2α, one β and one γ chain
Its level is increased in diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Hypnozoites are dormant liver-stage forms unique to Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale, which can remain latent in hepatocytes for months to years before reactivating to cause true relapse. P. malariae and P. falciparum do not form hypnozoites and therefore cannot cause true relapse.
questions.keyConcept: Hypnozoites (dormant liver forms causing true relapse) occur only in P. vivax and P. ovale.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: About HbAle which is incorrect?
options: It is formed of four subunits Fe*+
Its N-terminus ß chain is conjugated with glucose
Its level is increased in diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: The answer is C, because HbA1c is azß, and does not contain y chains. Option A, it is composed of four subunits, is true. Option B, the N-terminus of the B chain is conjugated with glucose, is true. Option D, its level is increased in diabetes mellitus, is true.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “About HbAle which is incorrect”, the defining choice is “It consists of 2a, 1 B & 1 y-chain”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is a tetrameter consisting of ________
questions.explanation: Normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) is a tetramer of two alpha and two beta chains (α2β2).
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is a tetrameter consisting of ________”, the defining choice is “α2β2”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Alpha chain in 1ry structure of hemoglobin contain ______ amino acids.
questions.explanation: A chancre (a firm, painless nodule at the tsetse fly bite site) is the primary skin lesion of African trypanosomiasis, appearing before systemic spread; this is distinct from the diffuse skin lesions of cutaneous leishmaniasis or the absence of a primary skin lesion in Chagas disease and toxoplasmosis.
questions.keyConcept: A chancre at the tsetse-fly bite site is the characteristic primary lesion of African trypanosomiasis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An important difference between Hb and Mb is that:
options: Hb is a heterotetramer formed of two alpha and two beta chains
Hb binds oxygen more tightly than Mb
Each chain of Hb contains heme
Polypeptides of Hb are folded mostly into α helices
questions.explanation: Both Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale cause enlargement of infected RBCs, since these species preferentially invade young/reticulocyte-stage red cells, which enlarge further as the parasite grows -- unlike P. falciparum (which infects RBCs of any age without notable enlargement) or P. malariae (which infects older/smaller RBCs).
questions.keyConcept: P. vivax and P. ovale enlarge the RBCs they infect because they preferentially invade young reticulocytes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hb A2 is a tetrameter consisting of ________
questions.explanation: Humans acquire Toxoplasma gondii infection by eating undercooked meat containing tissue cysts (bradyzoites), distinguishing this route from Trypanosoma cruzi (triatomine bug feces), kala azar (sandfly bite), and Wuchereria bancrofti (mosquito bite), none of which are meat-borne.
questions.keyConcept: Toxoplasma is uniquely acquired via ingestion of undercooked meat containing tissue cysts, unlike the vector-borne parasites listed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hb has higher affinity to O2 at all pO2 values than Myoglobin.
questions.explanation: This is false - myoglobin has a higher O2 affinity than hemoglobin at all oxygen tensions, which is why myoglobin can extract O2 from hemoglobin in muscle tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Hb has higher affinity to O2 at all pO2 values than Myoglobin.”, the defining choice is “False”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hb owes its buffering capacity to its high content of which amino acid?
questions.explanation: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa near physiological pH, making it an excellent buffer; hemoglobin is rich in histidine residues.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Hb owes its buffering capacity to its high content of which amino acid”, the defining choice is “Histidine”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Hemoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve (P50) is:
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin's P50 (the pO2 at half saturation) is approximately 26 mmHg under normal physiologic conditions.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In Hemoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve (P50) is”, the defining choice is “26 mm Hg”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Hemoglobin, pO2 needed to achieve 100% saturation is:
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin becomes essentially fully saturated with oxygen at the pO2 found in the lungs/arterial blood, approximately 100 mmHg.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In Hemoglobin, pO2 needed to achieve 100% saturation is”, the defining choice is “100 mm Hg”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In myoglobin, PO, needed to achieve half saturation of binding sites (Pso) is:
questions.explanation: Answer is A, as myoglobin's P50 is approximately 2-5 mmHg, indicating high oxygen affinity for storage. C, 26 mm Hg - FALSE because this is hemoglobin's P50.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In myoglobin, PO, needed to achieve half saturation of binding sites (Pso) is”, the defining choice is “5 mm Hg c. 26 mm Hg”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In myoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve 100% saturation of binding sites is:
questions.explanation: Because of its hyperbolic, high-affinity binding curve, myoglobin approaches full saturation at a relatively low oxygen tension of around 20 mmHg.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In myoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve 100% saturation of binding sites is”, the defining choice is “20 mm Hg”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In myoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve half saturation of binding sites (P50) is:
questions.explanation: Myoglobin's very high O2 affinity gives it a low P50 of about 5 mmHg, much lower than hemoglobin's P50 of about 26 mmHg.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In myoglobin, PO2 needed to achieve half saturation of binding sites (P50) is”, the defining choice is “5 mm Hg”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the binding of oxygen to Hemoglobin, the relationship between the concentration of oxygen and the fraction of binding sites occupied can best be described as:
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin's four subunits bind O2 cooperatively, producing a sigmoidal (S-shaped) oxygen saturation curve, in contrast to myoglobin's hyperbolic curve.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In the binding of oxygen to Hemoglobin, the relationship between the concentration of oxygen and the fraction of binding sites occupied can best be described as”, the defining choice is “Sigmoidal”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the binding of oxygen to myoglobin, the relationship between the concentration of oxygen and the fraction of binding sites occupied can best be described as:
questions.explanation: Unilateral eyelid/facial oedema (Romaña sign) together with cardiac arrhythmia and constipation (from destruction of cardiac and gut autonomic ganglia) in a South American patient is the classic clinical picture of acute-to-chronic Chagas disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi ('Monomorphic trypanosoma' in this course's terminology), not malaria, which does not produce Romaña sign or these autonomic manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Romaña sign plus cardiac/GI autonomic findings in a South American patient is diagnostic of Chagas disease (T. cruzi), not malaria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the binding of oxygen to myoglobin,9. the relationship between the concentration of oxygen & the fraction of binding sites occupied can best described as:
questions.explanation: binding. B, linear, is false because oxygen binding is not linear. C, sigmoidal, is also false, as this shape characterizes hemoglobin's cooperative binding.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In the binding of oxygen to myoglobin,9. the relationship between the concentration of oxygen & the fraction of binding sites occupied can best described as”, the defining choice is “Hyperbolic”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In which iron (Fe) state Hemoglobin binds to the oxygen?
questions.explanation: Both Plasmodium species and Babesia live inside red blood cells and destroy them directly through their intraerythrocytic asexual multiplication, producing hemolytic anemia; this distinguishes them from trypanosomes, which circulate extracellularly in plasma rather than inside RBCs.
questions.keyConcept: Plasmodium and Babesia both cause hemolytic anemia through direct intraerythrocytic red cell destruction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron can form coordination bonds in Hb with all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom's sign) together with irregular febrile attacks in a patient from West Africa is the classic clinical picture of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) caused by Trypanosoma gambiense, not malaria -- Plasmodium infection does not characteristically produce posterior cervical lymph node swelling.
questions.keyConcept: Winterbottom's sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy) with irregular fever in a West African patient is diagnostic of African trypanosomiasis, not malaria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Myoglobin and the subunits of hemoglobin have:
options: Very different primary and tertiary structures
Very similar primary and tertiary structures
Very similar primary structures, but different tertiary structures
Very similar tertiary structures, but different primary structures
questions.explanation: Myoglobin and hemoglobin subunits share the same globin fold (very similar tertiary structure/3D shape) despite having quite different amino acid sequences (primary structure) - a classic example of structural convergence in the globin family.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Myoglobin and the subunits of hemoglobin have”, the defining choice is “Very similar tertiary structures, but different primary structures”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: One hemoglobin carries __________ molecules of oxygen.
questions.explanation: Each hemoglobin tetramer has four heme groups, each capable of binding one O2 molecule, for a maximum of 4 O2 molecules carried per hemoglobin.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “One hemoglobin carries __________ molecules of oxygen.”, the defining choice is “4”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: P50 for hemoglobin is:
options: The O2 pressure at which hemoglobin is half saturated with oxygen
The O2 pressure at which hemoglobin is fully deoxygenated
questions.explanation: P50 is defined as the partial pressure of oxygen at which the protein is 50% saturated; for Hb this is about 26 mmHg, which is higher (not lower) than myoglobin's ~2-5 mmHg because Mb has greater O2 affinity.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “P50 for hemoglobin is”, the defining choice is “The O2 pressure at which hemoglobin is half saturated with oxygen”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The oxygen dissociation curve of hemoglobin is:
options: More affinity to O2 than Mb
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin's curve is sigmoidal because of cooperative binding between its four subunits; myoglobin's curve is hyperbolic and myoglobin has higher, not lower, O2 affinity than Hb.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “The oxygen dissociation curve of hemoglobin is”, the defining choice is “Showing cooperativity properties”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The structure of normal adult hemoglobin (HA) can be described
options: In acute iron toxicity, gastric lavage is performed with saline solutions
In chronic iron toxicity, Deferoxamine is given IM or SC
In Diphyllobothriasis, Praziquantel is used with Vitamin B12
In anemia of chronic disease, iron therapy is not required
questions.explanation: In acute iron toxicity, gastric lavage should use sodium bicarbonate solution (which helps precipitate iron and reduce absorption), not plain saline, making that statement incorrect; chronic iron toxicity is treated with deferoxamine (IM/SC), diphyllobothriasis (which can cause B12 deficiency) is treated with praziquantel plus B12 replacement, and anemia of chronic disease generally does not need iron therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium bicarbonate, not saline, is the correct gastric lavage solution for acute iron toxicity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What consists of 2 alpha chains and 2 gamma chains?
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi (the agent of Chagas disease) multiplies as amastigotes inside macrophages and other cells of the reticulo-endothelial system before differentiating into trypomastigotes that circulate in blood. This intracellular reticuloendothelial tropism distinguishes it from the African trypanosomes (T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense), which remain predominantly extracellular in blood and lymph.
questions.keyConcept: T. cruzi is unique among trypanosomes in multiplying intracellularly as amastigotes within reticuloendothelial cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: When oxygen binds to a heme-containing protein, the two open coordination bonds of Fe2+ are occupied by:
options: One O atom and one amino acid
One O2 molecule and one amino acid
One O2 molecule and one heme atom
questions.explanation: A pattern of periodic fever with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and jaundice that becomes progressively irregular over time is classically described for Plasmodium falciparum infection, whose fever paroxysms often start with a tertian (every-third-day) pattern before becoming irregular as multiple broods of parasites become asynchronous.
questions.keyConcept: Falciparum malaria fever classically starts periodic and becomes irregular as parasite broods lose synchrony.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors fixes the taut (T) form of Hb?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG preferentially binds and stabilizes the low-affinity taut (T, deoxy) conformation of hemoglobin, lowering its oxygen affinity; low H+, low CO2, and high oxygen all favor the relaxed (R) high-affinity state instead.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Which of the following factors fixes the taut (T) form of Hb”, the defining choice is “2,3-BPG”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is false?
options: Heme consists of a complex organic ring structure 'protoporphyrin'
Protoporphyrin is bound to a single iron in its Ferric Fe3+ state
Heme is found in a number of oxygen transporting proteins
questions.explanation: Functional heme iron is normally in the ferrous (Fe2+) state, not ferric (Fe3+); Fe3+ heme (as in methemoglobin) cannot bind oxygen. The other statements about protoporphyrin structure, 6 coordination bonds, and O2-transport proteins are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Which of the following is false”, the defining choice is “Protoporphyrin is bound to a single iron in its Ferric Fe3+ state”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the oxygen binding site of the hemoglobin?
options: Carboxyterminal of both alpha and beta subunits
Ferric ion (Fe3+) of the heme molecule
Ferrous ion (Fe2+) of the heme molecule
questions.explanation: Kala azar (visceral leishmaniasis) classically causes pancytopenia through hypersplenism and bone marrow infiltration by amastigotes, distinguishing it from Chagas disease, toxoplasmosis, and filariasis, which do not typically produce this triad of anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia together.
questions.keyConcept: Kala azar's hypersplenism and marrow infiltration classically produce pancytopenia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements about adult Hb (HbA) is true?
options: HbA is composed of two α and two γ chains
Each chain of HbA has one heme
HbA is more hydrophobic than hemoglobin S
HbA has higher affinity to O2 than hemoglobin F
HbA migrates slower than HbS in alkaline pH
questions.explanation: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic protozoan transmitted by ixodid ticks; it invades red blood cells directly with no hepatic schizogony phase, does not produce hemozoin pigment (unlike Plasmodium), and its ring forms can resemble P. falciparum on a blood film, occasionally causing diagnostic confusion.
questions.keyConcept: Babesia is correctly defined as a tick-borne, intraerythrocytic protozoan without a hepatic phase or hemozoin pigment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which statement concerning Hb is correct?
options: Fetal Hb has higher affinity for O2 because it can't bind 2,3-BPG as well
The chain composition of HbF is 2α & 2δ
HbA1c differs from HbA by a single amino acid
CO decreases the affinity of Hb to oxygen
questions.explanation: HbF (α2γ2) binds 2,3-BPG more weakly than HbA, giving it higher O2 affinity, which favors placental oxygen transfer to the fetus. HbF is α2γ2 not α2δ2; HbA1c is a glycated adduct, not a single-amino-acid variant; CO increases (not decreases) Hb's apparent O2 affinity by locking it in the R-state.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Which statement concerning Hb is correct”, the defining choice is “Fetal Hb has higher affinity for O2 because it can't bind 2,3-BPG as well”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ________ can indicate how the treatment is controlling the patient blood glucose over more than 4 months.
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis can present in the newborn with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and the classic triad of hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications, distinguishing it from kala azar, amoebic liver abscess, and Chagas disease, which are not typical causes of neonatal jaundice via transplacental infection.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital (transplacental) Toxoplasma infection can present with neonatal jaundice as part of its classic clinical picture.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Beta-thalassemia minor is characterized by_________
options: Defective mutation of one of two beta genes of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassemia minor (trait) involves a mutation in only one of the two beta-globin genes, and is characterized by compensatory increases in both HbA2 and HbF as the body partly compensates for reduced beta-chain production.
questions.keyConcept: Sporogony -- the mosquito-stage sexual reproduction producing sporozoites -- is the specific name for Plasmodium's cycle in the female mosquito.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hemoglobin H disease is characterized by the deletion of ________
questions.explanation: False relapse (recrudescence) results from incomplete eradication of blood-stage (erythrocytic) parasites rather than reactivation of dormant liver hypnozoites; it can occur with any Plasmodium species that persists at sub-patent levels in the blood, including P. falciparum and P. malariae. True relapse from hypnozoites, by contrast, is restricted to P. vivax and P. ovale.
questions.keyConcept: False relapse (recrudescence) arises from residual blood-stage parasites and can occur in any Plasmodium species, unlike hypnozoite-driven true relapse.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hydrops fetalis is a clinical condition caused by the deletion of the alpha genes of hemoglobin. Among a total of four alpha genes, the hydrops fetalis is caused by deletion of ________
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala azar) is characterized by a high ratio of subclinical to clinical infection: the majority of infections remain inapparent, with only a small fraction (roughly 3%) progressing to overt clinical kala azar, reflecting the importance of host immune status in determining disease expression.
questions.keyConcept: Visceral leishmaniasis has a high subclinical-to-clinical ratio, with only about 3% of infections becoming overtly symptomatic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Hb M, Proximal histidine in Beta chain is substituted with:
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin M variants arise from substitution of the proximal (or distal) histidine by tyrosine; the phenolic group of tyrosine stabilizes the heme iron in the oxidized ferric (Fe3+) state, which cannot bind oxygen.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In Hb M, Proximal histidine in Beta chain is substituted with”, the defining choice is “Tyrosine”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In HbC glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta-chain is replaced by:
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin C results from a glutamic acid to lysine substitution at position 6 of the beta chain, distinct from HbS (glutamic acid to valine at the same position).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In HbC glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta-chain is replaced by”, the defining choice is “Lysine”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In HbS, what will be the electrophoretic mobility towards the anode?
options: Depends on level of concentration of HbS
questions.explanation: The Glu->Val substitution in HbS removes a negatively charged residue, reducing the molecule's overall negative charge and causing it to migrate more slowly (decreased mobility) toward the anode compared to HbA on alkaline electrophoresis.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In HbS, what will be the electrophoretic mobility towards the anode”, the defining choice is “Decreased”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Hemoglobin electrophoresis:
options: HbA will be slower than HbS
Hb F will be faster than Hb A
Hb C will be the fastest
Hb S will be slower than Hb A
questions.explanation: On alkaline hemoglobin electrophoresis, HbA migrates fastest toward the anode (most negatively charged), while HbS (with its neutral valine substitution reducing negative charge) migrates more slowly; HbC migrates slowest of the common variants, not fastest.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In Hemoglobin electrophoresis”, the defining choice is “Hb S will be slower than Hb A”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Thalassemia the abnormality is related to:
options: the rate of synthesis of hemoglobin
an abnormal molecular structure of hemoglobin
questions.explanation: Thalassemias are quantitative disorders - they result from reduced or absent synthesis (production rate) of normal globin chains, unlike sickle cell disease, which is a qualitative (structural) hemoglobin defect.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In Thalassemia the abnormality is related to”, the defining choice is “the rate of synthesis of hemoglobin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In beta thalassemia major, which of the following globin chains will be increased?
questions.explanation: With little or no functional beta-chain production in beta-thalassemia major, the body compensates by increasing gamma- and delta-chain production, raising HbF and HbA2 levels.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “In beta thalassemia major, which of the following globin chains will be increased”, the defining choice is “gamma and delta”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In sickle cell disease the abnormality is related to:
options: the rate of synthesis of hemoglobin
an abnormal molecular structure of beta chain
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is a qualitative (structural) hemoglobinopathy - it results from an abnormal amino acid substitution altering the structure of the beta chain, not from reduced production rate as in thalassemia.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “In sickle cell disease the abnormality is related to”, the defining choice is “an abnormal molecular structure of beta chain”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder of hemoglobin synthesis. Identify the correct answer from the following:
options: caused by a mutation in the sixth position of the alpha chain (glutamic acid is replaced by isoleucine)
caused by a mutation in the sixth position of the beta chain (glutamic acid is replaced by isoleucine)
caused by a mutation in the sixth position of the alpha chain (glutamic acid is replaced by valine)
caused by a mutation in the sixth position of the beta chain (glutamic acid is replaced by valine)
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease results from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene causing substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta chain (not the alpha chain, and not isoleucine).
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder of hemoglobin synthesis. Identify the correct answer from the following”, the defining choice is “caused by a mutation in the sixth position of the beta chain (glutamic acid is replaced by valine)”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of genetic mutation causes formation of HbS?
options: Frame shift mutation in beta-globin gene
Splice site mutation in beta-globin gene
Single base mutation (missense) in beta-globin gene
Single base mutation (nonsense) in beta-globin gene
questions.explanation: HbS arises from a single-base missense mutation (GAG to GTG) in the beta-globin gene, changing codon 6 from glutamic acid to valine, without any frameshift, splicing defect, or premature stop codon.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which type of genetic mutation causes formation of HbS”, the defining choice is “Single base mutation (missense) in beta-globin gene”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: α-globin gene is present on chromosome _____
questions.explanation: The alpha-globin gene cluster is located on chromosome 16, while the beta-globin gene cluster is on chromosome 11.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “α-globin gene is present on chromosome _____”, the defining choice is “16”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the followings can be seen in iron overload except?
questions.explanation: In iron overload, transferrin becomes increasingly saturated, which actually decreases (not increases) the remaining unbound total iron binding capacity (TIBC); hemosiderin deposition, liver cirrhosis, and bronze diabetes are all recognized consequences of iron overload.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “All of the followings can be seen in iron overload except”, the defining choice is “Increase plasma iron binding capacity”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Bronze diabetes is due to ____
questions.explanation: 'Bronze diabetes' refers to hereditary hemochromatosis, in which chronic iron overload deposits in the skin (causing bronze discoloration) and pancreas (causing diabetes).
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Bronze diabetes is due to ____”, the defining choice is “Hereditary hemochromatosis”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Factors decrease absorption of iron include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C enhances (rather than decreases) iron absorption by reducing ferric to ferrous iron and forming soluble complexes; oxalates, phosphates, and phytates all bind iron and reduce its absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Factors decrease absorption of iron include all of the following except”, the defining choice is “Vitamin C”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Factors increase absorption of iron include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Phytates (found in plant foods/grains) bind iron and decrease its absorption; vitamin C, gastric acid, and increased physiologic demand during pregnancy all enhance iron absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Factors increase absorption of iron include all of the following except”, the defining choice is “Phytates”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: High intracellular iron causes all of the following except?
options: Activation of gene coding transferrin receptor
In liver this results in increased synthesis of hepcidin
questions.explanation: High intracellular iron actually suppresses (not activates) transferrin receptor expression via the IRE-IRP regulatory system, since less iron uptake is needed; it does increase ferritin synthesis (for storage), promote free radical formation (oxidative stress), and increase hepatic hepcidin synthesis (to limit further iron absorption).
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “High intracellular iron causes all of the following except”, the defining choice is “Activation of gene coding transferrin receptor”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the enterocytes, all of the followings are true except?
options: A divalent metal transport protein (DMT1) is present on the luminal surface of intestinal mucosa to transport iron exclusively
Iron is transported across the basolateral membrane of intestinal mucosa to circulation by ferroprotein (ferroportin)
Iron can be oxidized by ferroxidase to ferric and binds to apoferritin to make ferritin
Hepcidin synthesized in liver acts on intestinal cells inhibiting the gene of DMT and causing degradation of ferroportein in case of iron overload
questions.explanation: DMT1 is not iron-exclusive - it also transports other divalent metal ions such as zinc, copper, and manganese across the luminal enterocyte membrane, making statement (a) false; the other statements about ferroportin-mediated basolateral export, ferroxidase/apoferritin storage, and hepcidin's inhibitory action are all correct.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “In the enterocytes, all of the followings are true except”, the defining choice is “A divalent metal transport protein (DMT1) is present on the luminal surface of intestinal mucosa to transport iron exclusively”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron deficiency Anemia is the condition in which there is decreased hemoglobin and a clear deficiency of iron. Iron deficiency is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by decreased serum iron and ferritin (depleted stores) along with a compensatory increase in total iron binding capacity (TIBC), as the body upregulates transferrin in an attempt to capture more iron.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Iron deficiency Anemia is the condition in which there is decreased hemoglobin and a clear deficiency of iron. Iron deficiency is characterized by”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron is absorbed in _______
questions.explanation: Dietary iron is absorbed by enterocytes either as free ferrous iron (Fe2+, via DMT1) or as intact heme iron (via a separate heme transporter), making both (a) and (c) correct absorbable forms.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Iron is absorbed in _______”, the defining choice is “Both a and c”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron is transported in circulation bound to?
questions.explanation: Transferrin is the plasma glycoprotein that binds and transports iron through the circulation to tissues; ferroportin is a cellular exporter (not a plasma carrier), and DMT1/ceruloplasmin serve other roles in iron handling.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Iron is transported in circulation bound to”, the defining choice is “Transferrin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron overload can be caused by all of the following except?
questions.explanation: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) reduces iron absorption rather than causing overload; thalassemia, sickle cell anemia (via hemolysis and transfusion needs), and repeated blood transfusions are all recognized causes of iron overload.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Iron overload can be caused by all of the following except”, the defining choice is “Scurvy”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Iron overload may result from:
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic disease/sequestration involves iron being trapped within macrophages (functional iron deficiency despite adequate body stores), so it typically does not respond to routine oral ferrous sulfate the way true iron-deficiency anemia does.
questions.keyConcept: Iron sequestration in anemia of chronic disease does not respond to standard oral ferrous sulfate therapy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The average daily iron requirement is 15-20 mg/day.
questions.explanation: Because only about 10% of dietary iron is typically absorbed, a dietary intake in the range of roughly 15-20 mg/day is generally recommended to meet the body's much smaller actual absorption/replacement needs.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “The average daily iron requirement is 15-20 mg/day.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The intracellular iron is rapidly sequestered by ______
questions.explanation: Excess intracellular iron is rapidly bound and stored by ferritin, preventing free iron from catalyzing oxidative damage; transferrin is the extracellular/plasma transport protein, not an intracellular storage protein.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “The intracellular iron is rapidly sequestered by ______”, the defining choice is “Ferritin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The majority of iron in the body is present in______
questions.explanation: Of total body iron (~3-4 g), the largest fraction (about two-thirds) is found in hemoglobin within circulating red blood cells, far more than in transferrin, storage forms, or myoglobin.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “The majority of iron in the body is present in______”, the defining choice is “Hemoglobin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The only known exporter of iron from cells to blood is______
questions.explanation: Ferroportin is the sole known cellular iron exporter, releasing iron from enterocytes and macrophages into plasma; hepcidin regulates ferroportin (by causing its degradation) rather than exporting iron itself.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “The only known exporter of iron from cells to blood is______”, the defining choice is “Ferroportin protein”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The predominant storage form of iron in cells is ____
questions.explanation: Ferritin is the main, readily mobilizable storage form of intracellular iron; hemosiderin is a less accessible, aggregated storage form that accumulates when iron stores are excessive.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “The predominant storage form of iron in cells is ____”, the defining choice is “Ferritin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The total iron content of the human body is
questions.explanation: Total body iron content in a healthy adult is approximately 3-5 grams, mostly contained within hemoglobin.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “The total iron content of the human body is”, the defining choice is “3-5 g”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Total body Iron is regulated at the level of:
questions.explanation: Because the body has no active mechanism to excrete excess iron, total body iron balance is regulated almost entirely at the level of intestinal absorption (via hepcidin-ferroportin control), not by excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Total body Iron is regulated at the level of”, the defining choice is “Absorption”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where is hepcidin produced?
questions.explanation: Hepcidin, the master regulator of iron homeostasis, is synthesized in the liver and controls iron absorption/release by degrading ferroportin.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Where is hepcidin produced”, the defining choice is “Liver”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about iron absorption?
options: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum
Iron is absorbed in the ferrous form via DMT1
A ferrireductase enzyme is present on the surface of duodenal cells
Stomach hydrochloric acid & ascorbic acid convert ferrous iron to ferric
Hephaestin is present in the basal border
questions.explanation: Gastric HCl and ascorbic acid actually reduce ferric (Fe3+) iron to the more absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form, not the reverse; ferrireductase (duodenal cytochrome b) also performs this reduction before DMT1 transports Fe2+ into the enterocyte.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital malaria involves only the erythrocytic cycle in the newborn, since maternally transmitted parasites bypass the liver stage entirely.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following organ serves storage for cobalamin?
questions.explanation: Answer is A, as cobalamin is stored in large quantities in the liver, up to a six-year supply. B, Kidney - FALSE because the liver is the main storage organ. C, Spleen - FALSE because the liver is the main storage organ. D, Bone marrow - FALSE because the liver is the main storage organ.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Which of the following organ serves storage for cobalamin”, the defining choice is “Liver”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following are free radicals EXCEPT: due
questions.explanation: Administering erythropoietin injections directly stimulates erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow to increase red blood cell production, unlike the other listed conditions: increased blood oxygen reduces the hypoxic drive for erythropoiesis, gastric mucosa atrophy impairs intrinsic factor/B12 and iron absorption, erythroblastosis fetalis destroys RBCs, and folic acid deficiency impairs RBC maturation -- all of which decrease, not increase, red cell formation.
questions.keyConcept: Exogenous erythropoietin directly increases marrow RBC production, unlike the other listed conditions which all impair it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme produce hypochlerous acid?
questions.explanation: In iron deficiency anemia, insufficient iron limits hemoglobin synthesis during erythroid maturation, producing red cells that are both smaller than normal (microcytic) and paler than normal due to reduced hemoglobin content (hypochromic) -- the classic and most common anemia morphology.
questions.keyConcept: Iron deficiency anemia classically produces microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells due to impaired hemoglobin synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes need selenium:
questions.explanation: Answer is C, as the pathway is regulated to produce NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate as needed A, It generates NADH - FALSE because it generates NADPH B, It oxidizes NADPH to NADP+ - FALSE because it reduces NADP+ D, Glucose 6-phosphatase catalyzes the rate-limiting reaction of the pathway - FALSE because G6PD is rate-limiting
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which of the following enzymes need selenium”, the defining choice is “Glutathione peroxidase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A single gene for the β-globin chain is located on chromosome __
questions.explanation: In congenital infections, the newborn's own IgM and IgA (which cannot cross the placenta and therefore reflect fetal/neonatal production) are the key diagnostic markers of true intrauterine infection, whereas IgG can be maternally transferred across the placenta and does not by itself prove neonatal infection.
questions.keyConcept: Neonatal IgM/IgA (which cannot cross the placenta) specifically indicate true congenital infection, unlike maternally transferred IgG.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Arrange the following steps of gene evolution of globin chains: 1. transposition to two different chromosomes 2. mutation of two copies 3. duplication of the ancestral gene.
questions.explanation: Contrary to some other blood-feeding insects, both male and female Triatoma (kissing bugs) feed on blood -- the claim that 'only the female sucks blood' is therefore incorrect for Triatoma; the insect does have an incomplete life cycle, lives in cracks of poorly constructed housing, is unaffected by DDT, and feeds at night near the mouth, giving it the name 'kissing bug.'
questions.keyConcept: Unlike anopheline mosquitoes, both sexes of Triatoma feed on blood, making the 'only female feeds' statement false.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Globin types are originated first 'the ancestor' in DNA as:
questions.explanation: Morula cells (Mott cells) -- plasma cells distended with large globular accumulations of immunoglobulin (IgM) -- are a pathognomonic CSF finding in the meningoencephalitic stage of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) caused by T. gambiense/rhodesiense, reflecting intense intrathecal antibody production, and are not a feature of Chagas disease, visceral leishmaniasis, filariasis, or toxoplasmosis.
questions.keyConcept: Morula (Mott) cells in CSF are a pathognomonic finding specific to the meningoencephalitic stage of African trypanosomiasis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The α-gene cluster on chromosome ____ contains ______for the α-globin chains.
questions.explanation: American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease) is transmitted when triatomine ('kissing') bug feces, deposited near the bite wound, are rubbed into the skin or mucous membranes -- not through the insect's mouth/bite itself, unlike African trypanosomiasis (tsetse fly bite), filariasis (mosquito bite), toxoplasmosis (ingestion), or visceral leishmaniasis (sandfly bite), which do involve the vector's mouthparts or direct route.
questions.keyConcept: Chagas disease is transmitted via triatomine bug feces contaminating the bite wound, not via the insect's mouthparts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: α-Gene family has ______
questions.explanation: The DEC (diethylcarbamazine) provocative test increases peripheral microfilarial counts by mobilizing microfilariae from the lungs into peripheral blood, making it useful for diagnosing Wuchereria bancrofti infection when routine blood films are negative or when testing must be done outside the nocturnal periodicity window.
questions.keyConcept: The DEC provocative test mobilizes microfilariae into peripheral blood, aiding diagnosis of W. bancrofti when routine smears are negative.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: δ gene that codes for the globin chain found in the hemoglobin________
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis can damage the fetal central nervous system, producing hydrocephalus or microcephalus along with intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis, as part of its classic teratogenic triad -- a pattern not seen with T. cruzi, visceral Leishmania, W. bancrofti, or African trypanosomiasis.
questions.keyConcept: Hydrocephalus/microcephalus in a newborn is a classic CNS manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: ζ gene is expressed early in development as an α-globin-like component of ____ hemoglobin.
questions.explanation: Unlike Triatoma, in Glossina (tsetse fly) both males and females feed on blood, so the statement that 'only the female sucks blood' is incorrect; Glossina does have a complete life cycle, is an obligatory blood-feeding parasite, and G. morsitans is found in savanna while G. palpalis is found along forested riverbanks.
questions.keyConcept: Both sexes of Glossina (tsetse fly) feed on blood, making the 'only female feeds' statement false, unlike some other insects.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.topic: Molecular Biology of Hb Synthesis & Hemoglobinopathies
questions.lecture: Molecular Biology of Hb Synthesis & Hemoglobinopathies
questions.text: Globin types are originated first " ancestor" in DNA as:
options: Three genes in two chromosomes Chapter
