A, ALA synthase & Protoporphyrin oxidase - FALSE because ALA synthase is not inhibited. B, ALA synthase & Ferrochelatase - FALSE because ALA synthase is not inhibited. C, ALA dehydratase only - FALSE because ferrochelatase is also inhibited. 3 Molecular Biology of Hb Synthesis
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Globin types are originated first " ancestor" in DNA as”, the defining choice is “Three genes in two chromosomes Chapter”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All the following are Major Biochemical Features of Neutrophils except:
options: Unique enzymes as myeloperoxidase and NADPH oxidase
questions.explanation: Neutrophils rely mainly on active glycolysis and the HMP pathway for energy and NADPH (for the respiratory burst via NADPH oxidase and myeloperoxidase), and characteristically have relatively few mitochondria, not a high amount.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “All the following are Major Biochemical Features of Neutrophils except”, the defining choice is “high amount of mitochondria”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All the following are antioxidant except:
questions.explanation: NADPH oxidase generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide) as part of the respiratory burst to kill microbes, making it a pro-oxidant enzyme, unlike superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase, and catalase, which are antioxidant defenses.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “All the following are antioxidant except”, the defining choice is “NADPH Oxidase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All the following are free radicals except:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but is not itself a free radical, since it has no unpaired electron; superoxide and hydroxyl radicals are true free radicals with unpaired electrons.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “All the following are free radicals except”, the defining choice is “hydrogen peroxide”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Chronic granulomatous disease is due to mutation of:
questions.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase, impairing the respiratory burst and phagocytic killing of catalase-positive organisms, leading to recurrent infections and granuloma formation.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Chronic granulomatous disease is due to mutation of”, the defining choice is “NADPH Oxidase”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Collagenase enzyme is inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Alpha-2-macroglobulin is a broad-spectrum protease inhibitor that inhibits collagenase, among other proteases, protecting connective tissue from excessive proteolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Collagenase enzyme is inhibited by”, the defining choice is “α2-macroglobulin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Elastase enzyme is inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is the principal physiological inhibitor of neutrophil elastase, protecting tissues (especially lung) from proteolytic damage; its deficiency predisposes to emphysema.
questions.keyConcept: Link the molecule or pathway in the stem to its specific enzyme, cofactor, compartment, or regulatory step; for “Elastase enzyme is inhibited by”, the defining choice is “α1-anti-trypsin”.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme produce hydrogen peroxide?
questions.explanation: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide (and O2), which is subsequently detoxified by catalase or glutathione peroxidase, or used by myeloperoxidase to generate hypohalous acids.
questions.keyConcept: The oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway generates NADPH, which protects red cells by maintaining reduced glutathione; for “Which of the following enzyme produce hydrogen peroxide”, the defining choice is “Superoxide dismutase”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 48-year-old person has weakness, fatigue, bleeding gums and severe pancytopenia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Massive or rapid blood transfusion can cause immediate metabolic complications from citrate anticoagulant in stored blood: citrate chelates calcium (causing hypocalcemia) and its metabolism is impaired in massive transfusion, contributing to acidosis. Iron overload, diabetes, disease transmission, and hypertension are not typical immediate transfusion complications.
questions.keyConcept: Citrate in stored blood can cause immediate hypocalcemia and acidosis during large-volume transfusion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 66-year-old person develops macrocytic anemia and neurologic manifestations after gastrectomy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Naturally occurring ABO antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in a small volume of donor plasma are usually too dilute to cause significant hemolysis in the recipient's much larger blood volume unless present at unusually high titre, in which case even a modest volume of incompatible donor plasma can trigger a hemolytic reaction in the recipient.
questions.keyConcept: Donor plasma antibodies become clinically dangerous mainly at high titre, since dilution in recipient blood normally minimizes their effect.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A blood film shows leptocytes with target cells. This is most characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Target cells and thin leptocytes are classic in thalassemia because excess membrane relative to cell volume produces the target appearance.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “A blood film shows leptocytes with target cells. This is most characteristic of”, the defining choice is “Thalassemia”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient has stomatitis, microcytic anemia, brittle lusterless nails and koilonychia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency with dysphagia/stomatitis and koilonychia is characteristic of Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “A patient has stomatitis, microcytic anemia, brittle lusterless nails and koilonychia. What is the diagnosis”, the defining choice is “Plummer-Vinson syndrome”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with jaundice, gallstones and splenomegaly most likely has which type of anemia?
questions.explanation: An Rh-negative person lacks the D antigen on their RBC membrane and, unlike the ABO system, does not naturally form anti-D antibodies -- anti-D only develops after a sensitizing exposure to Rh-positive blood (via transfusion or pregnancy). A first-time exposure to Rh-positive blood is therefore not immediately dangerous, unlike ABO mismatches which involve pre-existing natural antibodies.
questions.keyConcept: Unlike ABO antibodies, anti-D is never naturally present; it forms only after an Rh-negative person is sensitized by Rh-positive blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Ankylostomiasis leads to:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (and folate) deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in dividing erythroid precursors, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation asynchrony (megaloblastic change) -- large, immature-nucleated precursors that die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) or release macrocytes. Hypoxia and iron deficiency instead affect the amount of hemoglobin made, not nuclear maturation, and bone marrow tumors cause space-occupying replacement rather than a maturation defect.
questions.keyConcept: B12/folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchronous) maturation of RBC precursors.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Aplastic anemia: all are true EXCEPT:
options: May result from bone marrow depression with some drug use
questions.explanation: Delayed complications of blood transfusion develop over a longer time course and include transfusion-transmitted infections and iron overload; repeated transfusions can lead to chronic liver iron deposition and eventually liver cirrhosis. Acute incompatibility reactions, jaundice from acute hemolysis, kidney shutdown, and hypotension are all immediate reactions occurring during or shortly after transfusion.
questions.keyConcept: Liver cirrhosis from chronic transfusional iron overload is a delayed complication, unlike acute hemolytic reactions or shock.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Both primary and secondary polycythemia are characterized by increased red blood cell count only.
questions.explanation: Living at high altitude causes hypoxia-driven secondary polycythemia (an increase in RBCs via erythropoietin), not anemia, distinguishing it from erythroblastosis fetalis, vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased kidney function (reduced EPO), and incompatible transfusion (hemolysis), which are all recognized causes of anemia.
questions.keyConcept: High altitude raises RBC mass (secondary polycythemia) rather than causing anemia, unlike the other listed conditions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Deficiency of vitamin B12 leads to:
questions.explanation: Advanced liver disease typically causes anemia (via bleeding, hypersplenism, or nutritional deficiency), not polycythemia. Renal/hepatic tumors can secrete ectopic erythropoietin, cyanotic heart disease and chronic pulmonary disease cause hypoxia-driven secondary polycythemia, and high altitude similarly stimulates compensatory erythropoietin release.
questions.keyConcept: Polycythemia occurs with hypoxia-driving conditions (cyanotic heart disease, lung disease, altitude) or EPO-secreting tumors -- not liver disease, which causes anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythroblastosis fetalis is characterized by:
options: Presence of antibodies from an Rh-negative mother in an Rh-positive infant
questions.explanation: Renal anemia results from insufficient renal erythropoietin production (since the kidney is the primary EPO source), so it is specifically treated by administering recombinant erythropoietin hormone to stimulate marrow red cell production, rather than iron, B12, folic acid, or bone marrow transplantation, which do not address the underlying EPO deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: Renal anemia is treated with erythropoietin replacement, addressing the underlying EPO deficiency directly.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythroblastosis fetalis may occur in infants with an Rh-positive father and an Rh-positive mother.
questions.explanation: A person whose plasma agglutinates both A and B red cells has antibodies against both A and B antigens (anti-A and anti-B), meaning their own RBCs carry neither antigen -- this defines blood group O, the universal RBC donor since O cells carry no A or B antigen to trigger a reaction in any recipient.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma agglutinating both A and B cells indicates group O blood, which lacks both A and B antigens on its own RBCs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythroblastosis fetalis occurs only in infants with an Rh-positive father and an Rh-negative mother.
questions.explanation: Classic Rh hemolytic disease requires an Rh-negative gestational parent carrying an Rh-positive fetus, usually inherited from an Rh-positive biological parent.
questions.keyConcept: Rh-negative people lack the D antigen and form anti-D only after sensitizing exposure; anti-D is not naturally present; for “Erythroblastosis fetalis occurs only in infants with an Rh-positive father and an Rh-negative mother.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Erythroblasts are never seen normally in the peripheral blood.
questions.explanation: In healthy older children and adults, nucleated erythroblasts remain in marrow; their peripheral appearance is pathologic.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Erythroblasts are never seen normally in the peripheral blood.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Favism is due to:
questions.explanation: In G6PD deficiency, oxidant compounds in fava beans cannot be neutralized adequately, causing acute intravascular hemolysis.
questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “Favism is due to”, the defining choice is “Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Gastrectomy leads to early iron deficiency anemia and late megaloblastic anemia.
questions.explanation: Loss of gastric acid may impair iron absorption early, while depletion of hepatic vitamin B12 stores after loss of intrinsic factor takes years and causes late megaloblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Gastrectomy leads to early iron deficiency anemia and late megaloblastic anemia.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hemolytic anemia is associated with increased serum bilirubin.
questions.explanation: Cross-matching directly tests donor RBCs against recipient serum (and vice versa) for agglutination, detecting any incompatibility beyond basic ABO/Rh typing before transfusion -- this is essential to prevent a major (acute intravascular) hemolytic transfusion reaction, the most dangerous transfusion complication. ESR, osmotic fragility, and bleeding time do not assess donor-recipient compatibility.
questions.keyConcept: Cross-matching detects donor-recipient incompatibility directly, preventing major hemolytic transfusion reactions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hemolytic anemia is not associated with gallstones.
questions.explanation: Chronic hemolysis increases bilirubin turnover and predisposes to black pigment gallstones.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Hemolytic anemia is not associated with gallstones.”, the defining choice is “False”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hemolytic anemia is not due to:
questions.explanation: Hemolytic anemia results from premature RBC destruction due to intrinsic or extrinsic causes. Bone-marrow hypofunction causes underproduction anemia rather than hemolysis.
questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “Hemolytic anemia is not due to”, the defining choice is “Bone marrow hypofunction”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by all EXCEPT:
options: Defect in the red blood cell membrane
Diminished life span of red blood cells
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant and results from an RBC membrane-skeleton defect that shortens cell survival. It causes hemolysis, not megaloblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP; for “Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by all EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Megaloblastic anemia”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In iron deficiency anemia, red blood cells do not show:
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency impairs hemoglobin synthesis, causing a production-type (microcytic hypochromic) anemia rather than hemolysis; it does not shorten red cell lifespan. In contrast, abnormal hemoglobin (e.g., sickle cell), congenital spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, and chemical poisons like arsenic all directly damage or destabilize red cells, causing true hemolytic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Iron deficiency causes anemia via impaired hemoglobin synthesis, not hemolysis, unlike the other listed causes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In iron deficiency anemia, red blood cells show:
questions.explanation: 1? Pathology of anemia & Polycythemia As Iron deficiency anemia typically presents as microcytic hypochromic anemia While anisocytosis and poikilocytosis are characteristic for vitamin b12 deficiency anemia and Normochromic appearance is wrong
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “In iron deficiency anemia, red blood cells show”, the defining choice is “Microcytic appearance”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In megaloblastic anemia, red blood cells do not show:
questions.explanation: In hemolytic anemia, accelerated red cell breakdown releases large amounts of hemoglobin that is converted to bilirubin, overwhelming hepatic conjugation capacity and causing elevated (unconjugated) bilirubin and jaundice -- unlike the other options, which describe changes opposite to what actually occurs in hemolysis (decreased O2 capacity, decreased RBC lifespan, increased not decreased erythropoietin, and normal iron absorption).
questions.keyConcept: Hemolytic anemia raises bilirubin and causes jaundice due to accelerated red cell breakdown overwhelming hepatic clearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Ingestion of fava beans may lead to aplastic anemia in some people.
questions.explanation: Fava beans trigger acute hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency, not aplastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Hemorrhagic (acute blood-loss) anemia does not itself raise bilirubin/cause jaundice, unlike hemolytic anemia, which does via accelerated RBC breakdown.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Leuco-erythroblastic anemia is due to bone marrow hypofunction.
questions.explanation: It is usually caused by marrow infiltration or fibrosis that forces immature myeloid and erythroid cells into blood, not simple hypofunction.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Leuco-erythroblastic anemia is due to bone marrow hypofunction.”, the defining choice is “False”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Leuco-erythroblastic anemia:
options: Occurs when bone marrow is replaced by another tissue such as metastatic tumor
May follow chloramphenicol or cytotoxic drugs
questions.explanation: Marrow replacement by metastatic tumor or fibrosis disrupts the marrow and releases immature myeloid and erythroid cells into blood, producing a leucoerythroblastic picture.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Leuco-erythroblastic anemia”, the defining choice is “Occurs when bone marrow is replaced by another tissue such as metastatic tumor”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Microcytic hypochromic anemia is seen in:
questions.explanation: As Iron deficiency anemia typically presents as microcytic hypochromic anemia While Folate and B12 deficiency cause macrocytic anemia, while sickle cell anemia and spherocytosis are typically normocytic
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Microcytic hypochromic anemia is seen in”, the defining choice is “Iron deficiency anemia”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Myelosclerosis leads to aplastic anemia.
questions.explanation: The supplied key marks this true; extensive marrow fibrosis can produce severe marrow failure with anemia and other cytopenias.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Myelosclerosis leads to aplastic anemia.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Pathological features of primary polycythemia include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency, intrinsic factor deficiency (impairing B12 absorption), and carbon monoxide poisoning (which functionally inactivates hemoglobin) all cause or mimic anemia. Living at high altitude instead stimulates erythropoietin and increases RBC mass (secondary polycythemia), the opposite of anemia.
questions.keyConcept: High altitude causes secondary polycythemia (increased RBCs), not anemia, unlike folate/intrinsic-factor deficiency or CO poisoning.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Polycythemia rubra vera is a neoplastic disease involving the normoblastic series of bone marrow.
questions.explanation: Polycythemia vera is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm with autonomous erythroid proliferation and usually panmyelosis.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Polycythemia rubra vera is a neoplastic disease involving the normoblastic series of bone marrow.”, the defining choice is “True”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Polycythemia rubra vera may be associated with:
questions.explanation: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm and may evolve into post-polycythemic myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukemia.
questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback; for “Polycythemia rubra vera may be associated with”, the defining choice is “Myeloid leukemia”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Presence of myelocytes and erythroblasts in the peripheral blood occurs in:
questions.explanation: Anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, producing tissue hypoxia that manifests as pallor, dizziness, muscle weakness, and low blood pressure; to compensate, the heart increases its workload (raising cardiac output and rate) rather than decreasing it, in an attempt to maintain tissue oxygen delivery.
questions.keyConcept: Anemia increases (not decreases) cardiac workload as a compensatory response to reduced O2-carrying capacity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Renal cell carcinoma may lead to polycythemia.
questions.explanation: Incompatible blood transfusion triggers an acute hemolytic reaction that can cause hemolytic jaundice, acute kidney shutdown (from free hemoglobin), capillary/microvascular blockage, and shock (from hypotension) -- but it causes hypotension, not hypertension, as part of the shock response.
questions.keyConcept: Incompatible transfusion causes hypotension/shock, not hypertension, as part of the acute hemolytic reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Sickle cell anemia is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia causes sickling, membrane damage and chronic hemolysis. It is a qualitative hemoglobinopathy rather than a primary reduction in the amount of hemoglobin synthesized.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Sickle cell anemia is characterized by all EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Decreased amount of hemoglobin”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Splenic infarction is common in:
questions.explanation: Repeated vaso-occlusion by sickled RBCs produces splenic infarctions and eventually functional autosplenectomy.
questions.keyConcept: Transferrin carries iron in plasma; ferritin stores intracellular iron; ferroportin exports iron from cells; for “Splenic infarction is common in”, the defining choice is “Sickle cell anemia”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Subacute combined degeneration occurs with which condition?
questions.explanation: Sensitization of an Rh-negative person refers to the immune response triggered by their first exposure to Rh-positive (D-antigen-bearing) red cells, whether via transfusion or during pregnancy/delivery of an Rh-positive fetus; this exposure induces production of anti-D antibodies, which pose a danger on any subsequent exposure to Rh-positive blood.
questions.keyConcept: Sensitization is the formation of anti-D antibodies after an Rh-negative person is first exposed to Rh-positive red cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Thalassemia is not characterized by:
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia results from bone marrow failure that suppresses production of all blood cell lines together -- red cells, white cells, and platelets (pancytopenia) -- rather than an isolated erythropoietin deficiency or a change limited to red cell size/number alone.
questions.keyConcept: Aplastic anemia is defined by pancytopenia -- deficiency of all marrow-derived blood cell lines, not just red cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following carcinoma may lead to polycythemia:
questions.explanation: Congenital spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, and G6PD deficiency all cause hemolytic anemia through intrinsic RBC membrane, hemoglobin structural, or enzyme defects that shorten RBC lifespan. Iron deficiency instead impairs hemoglobin synthesis (producing microcytic hypochromic anemia from reduced production), it does not shorten RBC survival or cause hemolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Iron deficiency causes anemia via reduced hemoglobin synthesis, not hemolysis, unlike spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, or G6PD deficiency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following type of anemia is common in the Mediterranean area:
questions.explanation: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) causes hemolytic anemia with hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, kernicterus, and hydrops (edema) from severe anemia/heart failure -- not polycythemia, since the underlying process is red cell destruction, not overproduction.
questions.keyConcept: Erythroblastosis fetalis produces hemolytic anemia and its consequences (jaundice, kernicterus, edema), not polycythemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to anemia only.
questions.explanation: B12 deficiency also causes neurologic dysfunction, including subacute combined degeneration, in addition to megaloblastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to anemia only.”, the defining choice is “False”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is NOT related to hemolytic anemia:
questions.explanation: ESR is a nonspecific test reflecting plasma protein changes (especially fibrinogen and globulins) during inflammation; it cannot pinpoint a specific disease but is valuable as a prognostic/monitoring test to track disease activity and progress over time, such as in rheumatic fever where it typically rises (not decreases) during active disease.
questions.keyConcept: ESR is best used as a nonspecific prognostic/monitoring test of inflammatory activity, not a diagnostic test for a specific disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which hemoglobin is diagnostic in sickle cell anemia?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin is an excellent physiological buffer because the imidazole groups of its histidine residues can accept or donate protons across physiologic pH ranges, helping buffer the carbonic acid produced from CO2 in tissues and stabilizing blood pH. Adult HbA is a2b2 (not a2g2, which is HbF), oxygen binding does not oxidize iron to the ferric state in normal function, and hemoglobin concentration is about 12-16 g/dl, not 79 g/dl.
questions.keyConcept: Hemoglobin's histidine imidazole groups make it a major physiological buffer for CO2-derived acid in the blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following disorders is considered as myeloproliferative disorder:
questions.explanation: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is calculated as (Hematocrit / RBC count) x 10; with HCT 30% and RBC count 2 x 10^6/mm3, MCV = (0.30 / 2,000,000) x 10^9 = 150 fL (given as 150 µ³ in this question's units), which is well above the normal range (80-100 fL), indicating macrocytic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Calculating MCV from HCT/RBC count here gives 150 fL, indicating macrocytic anemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Antimalarial drugs with possible harmful effects in pregnancy include:
questions.explanation: Primaquine is avoided because fetal G6PD status is unknown, and quinine requires cautious risk-benefit use.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Antimalarial drugs with possible harmful effects in pregnancy include”, the defining choice is “Primaquine and quinine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Artemisinin is NOT characterized by She following:
options: Used in treatment of multidrug resistant P. falciparum
Rapidly acting tissue schizonticide for all human malaria species
Cleavage of drug endoperoxide bridge associated with free radical production
Associated with serious cardiac complications (Prolonged QT Interval)
questions.explanation: As Primaquine does not prolong QT interval but its main risks are hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, methemoglobinemia, and Gl upset while other options are correct
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Artemisinin is NOT characterized by She following”, the defining choice is “Cleavage of drug endoperoxide bridge associated with free radical production”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Artemisinin is NOT characterized by:
options: Rapidly acting tissue schizonticide for all species
questions.explanation: Artemisinins are rapid blood schizonticides, not tissue schizonticides.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Artemisinin is NOT characterized by”, the defining choice is “Rapidly acting tissue schizonticide for all species”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Atovaquone is characterized by all EXCEPT:
options: Active against tissue and blood schizonts
Used for resistant falciparum prophylaxis and treatment
questions.explanation: Atovaquone is combined with proguanil, not pyrimethamine, for malaria.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Atovaquone is characterized by all EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Should be combined with pyrimethamine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Blackwater fever is associated with:
questions.explanation: Quinine-associated massive intravascular hemolysis can produce hemoglobinuria called blackwater fever.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Blackwater fever is associated with”, the defining choice is “Quinine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Blurred vision may occur with which antimalarial pair?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine causes retinal/corneal toxicity and quinine causes cinchonism with visual disturbance.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Blurred vision may occur with which antimalarial pair”, the defining choice is “Chloroquine and quinine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Blurring of vision may be occurred with the following pair of anti-malarial drugs:
questions.explanation: As Fansidar (pyrimethamine + sulfadoxine) is mainly a blood schizonticide with tissue schizonticide action and sporontocidal activity, but it is not a gametocidal
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Blurring of vision may be occurred with the following pair of anti-malarial drugs”, the defining choice is “Chloroquine & Quinine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cardiac conduction block is associated with:
questions.explanation: Atovaquone may be associated with cardiac conduction abnormalities in the source classification.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Cardiac conduction block is associated with”, the defining choice is “Atovaquone”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Chloroquine is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine kills erythrocytic schizonts and blocks heme detoxification but is not reliably gametocidal against P. falciparum.
questions.keyConcept: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis; for “Chloroquine is NOT characterized by”, the defining choice is “Gametocidal action against falciparum”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Chloroquine is used in all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis is treated with pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine; chloroquine is not standard therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Chloroquine is used in all the following EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Toxoplasmosis”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Choose the correct answer regarding primaquine:
options: Used in treatment of amoebic liver abscess. It induces radical cure in P. ovale & P.
It is the mainstay in treatment of non- relapsing malaria
questions.explanation: As Acute iron toxicity can be managed initially by gastric lavage with bicarbonate solution to precipitate ferric hydroxide and reduce absorption while Ferric iron is less well absorbed than ferrous iron, Hydroxocobalamin is preferred because it is more slowly released, not more rapidly absorbed, Ascorbic acid increases iron absorption, not reduces it and Folic acid supplementation is recommended for dialysis patients
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Choose the correct answer regarding primaquine”, the defining choice is “May induce corneal opacity”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Corneal opacity may occur with:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine accumulates in ocular tissues and can cause corneal deposits and retinal toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Corneal opacity may occur with”, the defining choice is “Chloroquine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Fansidar can play all the following roles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: As Artemisinin is Rapidly acting blood schizonticide for all human malaria species while it is Used in treatment of multidrug resistant P. falciparum, cleaves drug endoperoxide bridge associated with free radical production and associated with serious cardiac complications
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Fansidar can play all the following roles EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Blood schizonticide”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Fansidar has all the following roles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine acts mainly as a blood schizonticide and has causal/sporontocidal effects; it is not a gametocide.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Fansidar has all the following roles EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Gametocide”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Methemoglobinemia is associated with:
questions.explanation: Primaquine causes oxidant stress, producing methemoglobinemia and hemolysis, especially in G6PD deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin and lowers oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right; for “Methemoglobinemia is associated with”, the defining choice is “Primaquine”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Prolonged QT interval is associated with:
questions.explanation: Primary systemic (endemic) mycoses such as Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis, and Blastomyces dermatitidis are acquired by inhaling fungal conidia (spores) from contaminated soil or bird/bat droppings, initiating a pulmonary infection that may later disseminate. They are not spread person-to-person, by ingestion, or by direct skin inoculation (unlike some subcutaneous mycoses such as sporotrichosis).
questions.keyConcept: Primary systemic mycoses are acquired by inhaling environmental fungal conidia, not by person-to-person spread.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Regarding blood schizenticides, the incorrect sentence:
options: Fansidar is a combination of & pyrimethamine
questions.explanation: As Chloroquine is a blood schizonticide, concentrates in infected RBCs, and works by causing accumulation of toxic heme in the parasite, it has gametocidal activity only against P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae, but not against P. falciparum
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Regarding blood schizenticides, the incorrect sentence”, the defining choice is “Atovaquone could be combined proguanil”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Regarding blood schizonticides, choose the incorrect statement.
options: Atovaquone may be combined with proguanil
questions.explanation: Doxycycline is a slow-acting partner drug and should not be used alone to treat acute malaria.
questions.keyConcept: Match the drug to its molecular target, clinical indication, adverse-effect profile, and reversal strategy; for “Regarding blood schizonticides, choose the incorrect statement.”, the defining choice is “Doxycycline may be used alone”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is wrong as regard mechanism of action of antimalarial drugs:
questions.explanation: As Corneal opacity is a known side effect of chloroquine while other options don't cause Corneal opacity

questions.keyConcept: Plasmin's defining role is as an active proteolytic enzyme that breaks down fibrin (fibrinolysis).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: During erythropoiesis hemoglobin begins to accumulate in:
questions.explanation: The common pathway of both the extrinsic and intrinsic clotting cascades converges on the formation of prothrombin activator (prothrombinase complex), which then converts prothrombin to thrombin, which in turn converts fibrinogen to fibrin -- prothrombin activator formation is therefore the first step of the shared common pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Prothrombin activator (prothrombinase) formation is the first step of the shared common coagulation pathway.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: During erythropoiesis, at which stage is the nucleus extruded?

questions.keyConcept: Thromboxane A2 from activated platelets amplifies aggregation and granule release, the target of aspirin's antiplatelet effect.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: During hematopoiesis, the first stage at which cell self-renewal is stopped is:
questions.explanation: Platelets form the primary hemostatic plug, secrete vasoconstrictor chemicals (serotonin, thromboxane A2), provide a phospholipid surface (platelet factor 3) that supports the coagulation cascade, and retract the clot via their contractile proteins (actin/myosin) -- but activating plasminogen (fibrinolysis) is a function of tissue plasminogen activator from endothelium, not platelets.
questions.keyConcept: Activating plasminogen (fibrinolysis) is not a platelet function, unlike plug formation, vasoconstriction, coagulation support, and clot retraction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: First step in erythropoiesis to be released in blood is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C (Reticulocyte) because the reticulocyte is the first erythroid cell normally released from bone marrow into peripheral blood, where it matures into an erythrocyte. Earlier nucleated stages remain in marrow.
questions.keyConcept: Identify the cell or tissue by its microscopic morphology, granules, and functional specialization; for “First step in erythropoiesis to be released in blood is”, the defining choice is “Reticulocyte”.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Fixed cells of bone marrow include the following except:

questions.keyConcept: Identify the cell or tissue by its microscopic morphology, granules, and functional specialization; for “Fixed cells of bone marrow include the following except”, the defining choice is “Reticulocyte”.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In hematopoiesis, morphological differentiation begins in:

questions.keyConcept: Prostacyclin from intact endothelium actively inhibits platelet aggregation, confining clot formation to the injury site.

questions.keyConcept: Thrombin is the specific enzyme that converts fibrinogen into fibrin, forming the structural clot meshwork.

questions.text: Polycythemia is an increase in the number of:

questions.keyConcept: Platelet plug formation follows adhesion, then activation/release, then aggregation, in that specific order.

questions.text: A defect in one of the peripheral cytoskeletal proteins of erythrocytes would most likely produce:

questions.explanation: Thrombin activates fibrinogen, platelet aggregation, and factors V and VIII in a positive feedback loop that amplifies clot formation, but it does not activate factor III (tissue factor), which acts upstream in the extrinsic pathway to initially trigger coagulation rather than being a downstream thrombin target.
questions.keyConcept: Tissue factor (factor III) acts upstream of thrombin and is not itself activated by thrombin, unlike fibrinogen or factors V/VIII.

questions.text: Functions of RBCs include the following except:

Act as an excellent acid-base buffer

questions.explanation: Thrombin activates fibrinogen (to fibrin), platelet aggregation, and factors V and VIII (feedback amplification of the clotting cascade), but does not activate factor III (tissue factor/thromboplastin), which instead acts upstream of thrombin to trigger the extrinsic pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Thrombin amplifies clotting by activating fibrinogen, platelets, and factors V/VIII, but not tissue factor (factor III), which acts upstream.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In hereditary spherocytosis, the primary structural defect of RBCs occurs in:
questions.explanation: Serotonin, released from activated platelets (and also present in dense granules), causes local vasoconstriction of the injured vessel, reducing blood flow and blood loss during the vascular phase of hemostasis -- distinguishing it from antithrombin, fibrinogen, tissue factor, and calcium, which act primarily in coagulation rather than vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released serotonin mediates vasoconstriction of the injured vessel during the vascular phase of hemostasis.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In slow circulation RBCs tend to be arranged in:
questions.explanation: Hemostasis proceeds through an ordered sequence: (1) the vascular phase (vasoconstriction), (2) the platelet plug phase (platelet adhesion/aggregation), and (3) coagulation (clot formation) -- making the platelet plug phase the second step, following the initial vascular response.
questions.keyConcept: The platelet plug phase is the second step of hemostasis, following vasoconstriction and preceding coagulation.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Life span of RBCs is:
questions.explanation: The intrinsic coagulation cascade proceeds: (1) activated factor XII triggers the cascade, leading to (3) formation of prothrombin activator, which converts prothrombin to (4) thrombin, which finally converts fibrinogen to (2) fibrin -- this sequence reflects the stepwise amplification of the clotting cascade.
questions.keyConcept: The intrinsic pathway proceeds from factor XII activation through prothrombin activator and thrombin to final fibrin formation.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Poikilocytosis is:

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: RBCs in hypertonic solution undergo:

questions.keyConcept: Identify the cell or tissue by its microscopic morphology, granules, and functional specialization; for “The inner aspect of the RBC membrane is related to”, the defining choice is “Ankyrin and spectrin”.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for flexibility of RBCs?

questions.keyConcept: Identify the cell or tissue by its microscopic morphology, granules, and functional specialization; for “Which of the following is responsible for flexibility of RBCs”, the defining choice is “Spectrin lattice”.

questions.text: The most numerous type of white blood cell, whose primary function is phagocytosis, is
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Neutrophils. Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species. Applied to “The most numerous type of white blood cell, whose primary function is phagocytosis, is”: the discriminating answer is “Neutrophils”.
questions.keyConcept: ALA synthase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis and requires vitamin B6, not biotin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The neutrophil granulocytes:
options: Are immotile so they cannot leave the blood stream.
Are the least numerous leukocytes in the blood.
Have a life span of about 120 days.
Are the first line of defense against parasites.
questions.explanation: This is a correct statement, Neutrophil granules are essentially lysosomes filled with proteolytic enzymes, They kill bacteria by releasing these enzymes and by generating powerful oxidizing agents (like H,O,) via the respiratory burst, a, Are immotile so they cannot leave the blood stream - FALSE, They are highly motile and perform diapedesis, b, Are the least numerous leukocytes in the blood - FALSE, They are the most numerous, d, Have a life span of about 120 days - FALSE, Their lifespan is very short (hours in blood, a few days in tissues), 120 days is the lifespan of an RBC, e, Are the first line of defense against parasites - FALSE, That is the role of eosinophils.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “The neutrophil granulocytes”, the defining choice is “Contain lysosomes & oxidizing agents.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The process of adherence of WBCs to vascular wall is:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Margination. Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall; for “The process of adherence of WBCs to vascular wall is”, the defining choice is “Margination”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The process of attraction of WBCs to infected area is:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Chemotaxis. Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall; for “The process of attraction of WBCs to infected area is”, the defining choice is “Chemotaxis”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The process of coating of bacteria to be tasty to WBCs is:
questions.explanation: Opsonization is the process of marking or coating a pathogen with opsonins (like IgG or C3b), which makes it more recognizable and easier for phagocytic cells to engulf.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall; for “The process of coating of bacteria to be tasty to WBCs is”, the defining choice is “Opsonization.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The process of movement of WBCs by pseudopodia is:
questions.explanation: Amoeboid movement is the crawling-like motion used by white blood cells to move through tissues, It is achieved by extending projections of the cytoplasm called pseudopodia.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall; for “The process of movement of WBCs by pseudopodia is”, the defining choice is “Chemotaxis.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The process of squeezing of WBCs through vascular wall is:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Diapedesis. Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte migration along a chemical gradient; diapedesis is passage through the vessel wall; for “The process of squeezing of WBCs through vascular wall is”, the defining choice is “Diapedesis”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The white blood cells, which directly kill virus infected cells and tumor cells, in are:
questions.explanation: This is the function of a specific subset of T-lymphocytes called cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CTLs or CD8* T cells), They recognize and directly kill host cells that are infected with viruses or have become cancerous.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “The white blood cells, which directly kill virus infected cells and tumor cells, in are”, the defining choice is “T-Lymphocytes.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The white blood cells, which include B cells and T cells, are
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Lymphocytes. Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “The white blood cells, which include B cells and T cells, are”, the defining choice is “Lymphocytes”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The white blood cells, which process antigens to present them, are:
questions.explanation: Macrophages are professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs), They phagocytose pathogens, break them down (process them), and present fragments (antigens) on their surface via MHC molecules to activate T-lymphocytes, e, B-Lymphocytes - TRUE (but Macrophages are the classic answer), B-cells are also APCs, but macrophages are the primary phagocytic APCs.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “The white blood cells, which process antigens to present them, are”, the defining choice is “Macrophages.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The white blood cells, which produces antibodies, are

questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “The white blood cells, which produces antibodies, are”, the defining choice is “B-Lymphocytes”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which chemical is NOT secreted by basophils?
questions.explanation: This chemical is not secreted by basophils, Protein C is a plasma protein synthesized by the liver that acts as a natural anticoagulant, a, b, c, d - TRUE, Histamine, Serotonin, Kinins, and SRS-A (leukotrienes) are all inflammatory mediators released or generated by activated basophils.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B6 (PLP) deficiency from isoniazid impairs ALA synthase, the first step of heme synthesis, causing sideroblastic-type anemia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of basophils:
options: Involved in urticarial and anaphylactic shock.
Release of heparin, histamine, serotonin and bradykinin.
Release of slowly reacting substances of anaphylaxis.
questions.explanation: This statement is false, Basophils are not phagocytic cells, Their primary function is to release the contents of their granules to mediate inflammatory and allergic reactions, a, b, c, d - TRUE, These all correctly describe the roles and secretions of basophils in Type I hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Heparin potentiates antithrombin and acts rapidly in vivo and in vitro; unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT; for “Which of the following is NOT a function of basophils”, the defining choice is “Involved in urticarial and anaphylactic shock.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a is chemotactic factor:
questions.explanation: This statement is false, Immunoglobulins (antibodies) are not chemotactic factors themselves, They act as opsonins to enhance phagocytosis, a, Toxins - TRUE, Bacterial toxins are potent chemoattractants, b, Inflamed tissues - TRUE, Damaged tissues release chemical signals, c, Complement 5 - TRUE, Specifically, the complement component C5a is a powerful chemotactic agent,
questions.keyConcept: Identify the normal mechanism first, then reject options that describe a different cell type, pathway, or regulatory response; for “Which of the following is NOT a is chemotactic factor”, the defining choice is “Immunoglobulins.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a the reticuloendothelial system?
questions.explanation: This statement is false, A proerythroblast is a red blood cell precursor, The reticuloendothelial system is a network of phagocytic cells, primarily monocytes and macrophages, found throughout the body, a, Liver Kupffer cells - TRUE, These are the resident macrophages of the liver, b, Pulmonary alveolar macrophages - TRUE, These are the resident macrophages of the lungs, c, Bone osteoclasts - TRUE, These are macrophage-like cells responsible for bone resorption, d, Brain microglia - TRUE, These are the resident immune cells (macrophages) of the central nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: Identify the normal mechanism first, then reject options that describe a different cell type, pathway, or regulatory response; for “Which of the following is NOT a the reticuloendothelial system”, the defining choice is “Liver Kupffer cells.”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a phagocytic cell:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Neutrophils. Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species. Applied to “Which of the following is a phagocytic cell”: the discriminating answer is “Neutrophils”.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils kill phagocytosed microbes using granule enzymes and an NADPH-oxidase respiratory burst that generates reactive oxygen species; for “Which of the following is a phagocytic cell”, the defining choice is “Neutrophils”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an important phagocytic cell:
questions.explanation: ALA synthase catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme biosynthesis, condensing succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid; it requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), not biotin, as its coenzyme, occurs in the mitochondria (not cytosol), and is not itself the enzyme classically inhibited by lead (lead instead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, later steps in the pathway).
questions.keyConcept: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting, B6-dependent, mitochondrial enzyme starting heme synthesis -- distinct from the lead-sensitive downstream enzymes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an opsonin:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Both B and C. IgG and C3b are major opsonins that enhance phagocyte recognition and ingestion.
questions.keyConcept: IgG and C3b are major opsonins that enhance phagocyte recognition and ingestion; for “Which of the following is an opsonin”, the defining choice is “Both B and C”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of these substances activates the fibrinolytic system:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Thrombin. Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback. Applied to “Which of these substances activates the fibrinolytic system”: the discriminating answer is “Thrombin”.
questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback; for “Which of these substances activates the fibrinolytic system”, the defining choice is “Thrombin”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: cell mediated immunity:

is accompanied with increase formation of plasma cell
occurs when foreign tissue is grafted to body
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** occurs when foreign tissue is grafted to body. B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity.
questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “cell mediated immunity”, the defining choice is “occurs when foreign tissue is grafted to body”.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: humoral immunity is the major defense against bacterial infections By following except:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** engulf bacteria. Identify the normal mechanism first, then reject options that describe a different cell type, pathway, or regulatory response.
questions.keyConcept: Identify the normal mechanism first, then reject options that describe a different cell type, pathway, or regulatory response; for “humoral immunity is the major defense against bacterial infections By following except”, the defining choice is “engulf bacteria”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old with bleeding gums, subconjunctival bleeding, purpura and more than 100,000 immature leukocytes/mm3 most likely has:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum (bound to intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells), not the duodenum. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin release, and ionizing radiation damages the bone marrow, reducing all blood cell lines -- these three statements are true.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum via intrinsic factor, not the duodenum (where iron is absorbed).

questions.explanation: As 9-year-old with fever, pneumonia, pallor, WBC 100,000/uL, mostly lymphoblasts, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly hallmark of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), the most common leukemia in children. While other choices are irrelevant

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 9-year-old patient with high remittent fever & pneumonia, severe pallor, of CBC showed leukocytes 100000/dl mostly lymphoblasts, pancytopenia, Hepatosplenomegaly, what is your diagnosis:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Causes of lymphocytosis are all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Whooping cough and infectious mononucleosis cause lymphocytosis; chronic infections such as tuberculosis may also do so. An acute bacterial lung abscess more typically causes neutrophilia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chronic lymphatic leukemia has a worse prognosis than chronic myeloid leukemia.
questions.explanation: Blood transfusion can transmit blood-borne infectious agents present in donor blood, such as HIV/AIDS, malaria parasites, syphilis (Treponema pallidum), and hepatitis viruses, all of which can circulate in donor blood or plasma. Cyanotic heart disease is a cardiac structural condition, not an infectious agent, so it cannot be transmitted through transfusion.
questions.keyConcept: Only infectious agents circulating in donor blood (HIV, malaria, syphilis, hepatitis) can be transfusion-transmitted; cyanotic heart disease is not infectious.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback; for “Chronic myeloid leukemia is associated with all of the following EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Anemia.”.

questions.text: Lymphocytosis occurs in:

questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Lymphocytosis occurs in”, the defining choice is “Viral infections”.

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Predisposing factors of leukemia include all EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Bacterial infections”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is not a cause of neutropenia:
questions.explanation: Typhoid, malaria and hypersplenism can reduce circulating neutrophils; lead poisoning is not a typical cause of neutropenia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The most important feature of chronic lymphatic leukemia is:

options: Marked generalized enlargement of lymph nodes
questions.explanation: CML often produces massive splenomegaly from sequestration and extramedullary hematopoiesis; generalized lymphadenopathy is more characteristic of lymphoid disease.
questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “The most important feature of chronic myeloid leukemia is”, the defining choice is “Markedly enlarged spleen”.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The total white cell count is markedly higher in chronic myeloid leukemia than chronic lymphoid leukemia.
questions.explanation: O-negative blood lacks A, B, and D (Rh) antigens on its RBCs, so it will not trigger an ABO or Rh-mediated reaction in a recipient of any blood type, making O- the universal RBC donor. questions.subject: Pathology

questions.text: Infectious mononucleosis is a:
questions.explanation: Anemia reduces blood viscosity (since viscosity depends heavily on hematocrit/RBC mass) and reduces O2-carrying capacity, causing pallor of mucous membranes; to compensate for reduced O2 delivery, cardiac output typically increases (not decreases), raising -- not lowering -- cardiac workload.
questions.keyConcept: Anemia raises (not lowers) cardiac output as a compensatory response, while it lowers blood viscosity and O2 carriage.

questions.text: Metastatic tumors in lymph nodes are not a cause of generalized lymph-node enlargement.
questions.explanation: Folic acid, vitamin B12, iron, and cobalt (as part of the B12 corrin ring) are all essential nutrients for normal RBC formation and hemoglobin synthesis. Calcium plays no essential role in erythropoiesis; it instead functions in coagulation, muscle contraction, and neurotransmission.
questions.keyConcept: Calcium is not required for erythropoiesis, unlike folate, B12, iron, and cobalt.

questions.explanation: A reduced albumin-to-globulin (A/G) ratio classically reflects chronic liver disease, where impaired hepatic synthetic function lowers albumin production while globulins may rise (e.g., due to chronic antigenic stimulation in cirrhosis), making the A/G ratio a useful indirect marker of hepatic synthetic capacity rather than of cardiac, pulmonary, neurological, or purely hypoxic conditions.
questions.keyConcept: A falling A/G ratio reflects reduced hepatic albumin synthesis, making it a marker specifically of liver disease.

questions.text: The commonest cause of splenomegaly is:
questions.explanation: Hemolytic disease of the newborn occurs when an Rh-negative mother (previously sensitized to the D antigen) carries an Rh-positive fetus; maternal anti-D crosses the placenta and hemolyzes fetal RBCs, releasing bilirubin that can cross the immature blood-brain barrier and deposit in the basal ganglia, causing kernicterus. This condition has been made rare by giving Rh-negative mothers anti-D immunoglobulin shortly after each delivery/exposure to prevent sensitization.
questions.keyConcept: Kernicterus in hemolytic disease of the newborn results from unconjugated bilirubin crossing the immature blood-brain barrier after Rh-mediated fetal hemolysis.

questions.text: The following type of lymphadenitis may be misdiagnosed as lymphoma:
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by the kidneys (about 85-90%) in response to tissue hypoxia, with only a small fraction (roughly 10-15%) contributed by the liver -- not the reverse. Vitamin B12 is essential for DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors, hypoxia (e.g., at high altitude) stimulates erythropoiesis, and bone marrow irradiation suppresses it -- these three statements are true.
questions.keyConcept: The kidney is the dominant source (~85-90%) of erythropoietin, with only a minor hepatic contribution.

questions.explanation: Plasma (the cell-free fluid portion of blood) excludes red blood cells by definition, so RBCs cannot be the answer to a question about plasma viscosity specifically (they do drive whole blood viscosity, which is a separate concept). Among the true plasma solutes, fibrinogen is the classic teaching answer for the main contributor to plasma viscosity, owing to its large, elongated molecular shape, which has an outsized effect on flow resistance relative to its concentration -- more so than the more abundant but more compact albumin.
questions.keyConcept: Fibrinogen's elongated shape gives it an outsized effect on plasma viscosity, distinguishing it from whole-blood viscosity (driven by RBCs).

questions.explanation: Histologic subtype influences prognosis, although stage and other clinical factors are especially important.

questions.text: Classic Reed-Sternberg cells are NOT:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and macrophages generate reactive oxidative bactericidal agents during the respiratory burst, including hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hypochlorite (via myeloperoxidase), and hydroxyl radicals (OH-) -- all of these contribute to intracellular killing of phagocytosed bacteria.
questions.keyConcept: Phagocytic respiratory burst generates multiple bactericidal oxidants together: H2O2, hypochlorite, and hydroxyl radicals.

questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “Mycosis fungoides is”, the defining choice is “T-cell lymphoma of the skin”.

questions.explanation: Immediate dangers of blood transfusion include mechanical circulatory overloading (from excessive volume/rate), citrate intoxication (causing hypocalcemia from the anticoagulant in stored blood), and acute renal shutdown (from hemoglobinuria in a hemolytic reaction). Hypernatremia is not a recognized immediate transfusion danger; citrate toxicity classically causes hypocalcemia, not sodium disturbance.
questions.keyConcept: Immediate transfusion dangers include volume overload, citrate-induced hypocalcemia, and acute renal shutdown -- not hypernatremia.

questions.keyConcept: Match the morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical pattern before selecting the diagnosis or mechanism; for “The following is an intermediate-grade lymphoma”, the defining choice is “Diffuse mixed small- and large-cell lymphoma”.

questions.explanation: Brucella survives and replicates inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion, which is its principal virulence mechanism, rather than relying on a classic exotoxin, capsule, or fimbriae.

severe increase in blood pressure occurs due to bacterial toxins
