questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old cattle farm worker experiences 6 weeks of undulating fever.19. The causative organism has a tropism for organs rich in which sugar, leading to abortion and mastitis in animals?
questions.explanation: Brucella has a tropism for erythritol-rich tissues such as the placenta and mammary gland, which is why it causes abortion and mastitis in cattle; erythritol promotes bacterial growth in these tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Brucella’s tropism for erythritol-rich tissue explains its reproductive/mammary pathology in livestock.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old farmer is bitten by a flea & 5 days later, he develops swollem, necrotic lymph nodes in the right axilla & groin, which are painful. One week later, he develops gangrene in the hands. What is the virulence factor involved in this complication?
questions.explanation: Pneumonic plague is acquired by inhaling infectious respiratory droplets, not by flea bite, so this statement is the false one. Wild rodents as the source, proventriculus blockage, regurgitation of infected blood, and high infectivity are all accurate features of Y. pestis transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumonic plague spreads via respiratory droplets, unlike bubonic plague, which spreads via flea bite.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old rabbit hunter to the room emergency lymphadenopathy & a skin lesion, started as a painful papule at of tick bite. The papule then Aspirate of the ulcer is positive ve bacilli. What is the main factor responsible for symptoms?
questions.explanation: This ulceroglandular presentation after a tick bite in a rabbit hunter is classic tularemia (Francisella tularensis), a facultative intracellular organism whose main virulence mechanism, like Brucella, is survival inside macrophages, evading intracellular killing.
questions.keyConcept: Francisella tularensis, like Brucella, is a facultative intracellular pathogen that survives within macrophages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer complains of extreme 8. weakness, a daily rise & fall in fever & night sweats, small gram-negative rods are isolated from blood cultures after a 2-week incubation period. What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: Undulant fever with night sweats and small gram-negative rods growing slowly (about 2 weeks) from blood culture in a farmer is the classic presentation of brucellosis caused by Brucella abortus (from cattle). Rickettsia does not typically grow in standard blood culture, and the Borrelia species cause relapsing fever with a different organism morphology and clinical course.
questions.keyConcept: Slow-growing small gram-negative rods from blood culture in a farmer with undulant fever indicate Brucella infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Because Brucella are intracellular pathogens, they are best treated with which of the following antibiotics:
questions.explanation: Dengue fever is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (primarily Aedes aegypti), but among the given pairings, the correct vector-disease blend is Dengue fever with Culex is false -- actually Rift Valley fever is transmitted by Culex/Aedes species, yellow fever by Aedes, and viral encephalitides (e.g., Japanese encephalitis) often by Culex, not Mansonia. Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles, not Aedes.
questions.keyConcept: Vector-disease pairings must match exactly: Aedes-yellow fever/dengue, Culex-viral encephalitis/Rift Valley fever, Anopheles-malaria, Mansonia-filariasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Plague is known as "Black death" because of
questions.explanation: Plague earned the name 'Black Death' because septicemic plague causes disseminated intravascular coagulation and subcutaneous hemorrhage, producing blackened, necrotic (gangrenous) skin, especially on the extremities.
questions.keyConcept: The historical name “Black Death” reflects the skin blackening seen in septicemic plague.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Yops (Yersinia outer proteins) are a group of virulence factors in Y. pestis that are injected into human cells to:
options: Cause lysis of the cell membrane
Form a protective capsule around the bacterium
questions.explanation: Yersinia pestis expresses a temperature-dependent coagulase/plasminogen activator (Pla) that has coagulase activity at the flea's cooler body temperature (20-28°C), promoting proventricular blockage, and switches to fibrinolytic activity at mammalian host temperature (35-37°C), promoting systemic spread after transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Y. pestis’s Pla protein switches from coagulase to fibrinolytic activity depending on ambient temperature.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which Yersinia pestis virulence factor is a plasminogen activator that has cougulase activity at the flea's temperature (20-28°C) and fibrinolytic (35-37°C)? activity at the host's temperature
questions.explanation: Pneumonic plague, spread via respiratory droplets from person to person, is the form most feared as a bioterrorism agent because it can cause rapid, direct human-to-human spread, unlike the flea-borne bubonic and septicemic forms.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumonic plague’s droplet-based person-to-person spread makes it the main bioterrorism concern.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which form of plague is communicable from person to person and poses a threat as a bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation: The gangrene seen in advanced (septicemic) plague results from endotoxin (LPS)-triggered septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, which causes thrombosis and necrosis of peripheral tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Endotoxin-driven DIC and septic shock in septicemic plague cause peripheral gangrene.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common form of plague which begins by swelling of the lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Yersinia pestis can be transmitted through flea bites (bubonic form), direct contact with infected rodents, and inhalation of respiratory droplets (pneumonic form), so all of the listed routes are valid.
questions.keyConcept: Y. pestis has multiple transmission routes: flea bite, direct animal contact, and respiratory droplets.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Y. pestis can be transmitted through: by
options: Direct contact with an infected rodent
inhalation of droplets from an infected patient
questions.explanation: Inside the flea's gut, Yersinia pestis expresses a temperature-dependent coagulase (active at the flea's ambient temperature of about 20-28°C) that promotes biofilm/clot formation, blocking the proventriculus and forcing the flea to regurgitate infected blood when it bites.
questions.keyConcept: Coagulase activity at flea-body temperature blocks the proventriculus, driving transmission via regurgitation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Yersinia pestis is characterized by of the followings:
options: It grows on sulphite blood agar
questions.explanation: The fastest recognized method for diagnosing plague is direct detection of the Yersinia pestis F1 capsular antigen using direct immunofluorescence, which gives a rapid, specific result compared with culture-based methods.
questions.keyConcept: Direct immunofluorescent detection of the F1 capsular antigen is the classic rapid diagnostic method for plague.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: factors Which is of produced the following by Yersinia virulence pestis in flea?
questions.explanation: Bubonic plague, which begins with painful swelling of regional lymph nodes (buboes) after a flea bite, is by far the most common clinical form of plague.
questions.keyConcept: Bubonic plague, marked by swollen lymph nodes, is the most common form of the disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: of Which transmission of the following of Y. pestis? isn't a character
options: Source of infection is wild rodents
Blocks the proventriculus of rat flea
1r pneumonic plague is acquired via flea bite
questions.explanation: Within the flea, at the cooler ambient temperature (about 20-28°C), Yersinia pestis expresses a temperature-dependent coagulase that promotes proventricular blockage; F1 capsule and Yops are instead expressed mainly at mammalian body temperature (37°C) during host infection.
questions.keyConcept: Coagulase expression in the flea vector is temperature-regulated and distinct from mammalian-phase virulence factors like F1 capsule and Yops.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 10 year old girl has leukemia & is receiving chemotherapy through an indwelling IV catheter. She now has a fever of 39 °C. Her blood culture shows growth of Gram +ve cocci, which is catalase + ve & coagulase-ve. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: In a neutropenic patient with an indwelling central venous catheter and yeast growing from blood culture, Candida species are the most common cause of catheter-associated fungemia, far more often than Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis (which does not typically grow in blood culture), or Histoplasma.
questions.keyConcept: Candida species are the leading cause of catheter-associated bloodstream fungal infection in neutropenic patients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old male who works poultry farm and suffers from leukemia presents with fever of difficulty in breathing. The illness with flu like symptoms and progressed to cough & dyspnea. A needle of lung tissue shows oval yeast alveolar macrophage. What etiology of this man's disease?
questions.explanation: Retroviruses characteristically integrate their genome into host cell DNA, and this integration can disrupt or mutate host regulatory genes (insertional mutagenesis), a defining oncogenic mechanism distinguishing retroviruses from other classes of oncogenic viruses.
questions.keyConcept: Retroviral genome integration into host DNA can mutate regulatory genes, driving malignant transformation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A neutropenie patient with an indwelling central venous catheter develops a fever. Blood cultures grow yeast. This bloodstream infection is most commonly caused by which opportunistic fungus?
questions.explanation: Candidal endocarditis is most frequently associated with growth of yeast and pseudohyphae on prosthetic heart valves (also seen with IV drug use and indwelling catheters), rather than on structurally normal, undamaged native valves.
questions.keyConcept: Candidal endocarditis is classically linked to prosthetic heart valves rather than normal native valves.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with came to the complaining of non-productive on examination he had splenomegaly, a blood smear was taken from showed intracellular yeast cells macrophage, which of the would be the causative agent case?
questions.explanation: EBV drives Burkitt's lymphoma by persisting latently in B cells with its genome maintained (episomally, with some genomic interactions) and by expressing latent viral proteins that promote continued B cell proliferation, rather than by replicating in monocytes/macrophages or producing toxic metabolites.
questions.keyConcept: EBV causes malignant transformation through persistent latent infection of B cells expressing oncogenic viral proteins.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Candidal endocarditis, severe opportunistic infection, is frequently associated with the growth of yeast and pseudohyphae on which site?
questions.explanation: Exposure to poultry/bird droppings with a subacute pulmonary illness and oval intracellular yeast forms within alveolar macrophages is classic for Histoplasma capsulatum, which is strongly associated with bird and bat droppings and can disseminate in immunocompromised hosts such as leukemia patients.
questions.keyConcept: Histoplasma capsulatum is classically linked to bird/bat dropping exposure and intracellular yeast in macrophages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Primary systemic mycoses are typically acquired through which route?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum has a truly global geographic distribution (found across the Americas, Africa, and Asia), unlike Coccidioides immitis (restricted to the arid southwestern US), Blastomyces dermatitidis (endemic to eastern North America), and Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (limited to Central and South America).
questions.keyConcept: Histoplasma capsulatum is unique among the primary systemic fungi for its worldwide distribution.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following primary systemic fungi is described as having a global geographical distribution?
questions.explanation: Small intracellular yeast forms seen within macrophages on a blood or tissue smear, together with splenomegaly and chronic respiratory symptoms, are the classic findings of disseminated histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum).
questions.keyConcept: Intracellular yeast within macrophages is the classic microscopic finding in histoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following describe rickettsia EXCEPT?
options: Affect endothelial cells of blood vessels
Can grow on enriched culture media
Serology has important rule in diagnosis
Phospholipase is an important virulence factor
questions.explanation: Recurrent, cyclical fevers after a tick bite are characteristic of tick-borne relapsing fever, in which each relapse is driven by successive antigenic variation of the spirochete's surface proteins, allowing it to evade the immune response generated against the previous variant.
questions.keyConcept: Each relapse in relapsing fever reflects a new antigenic variant of Borrelia evading prior immunity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Many survivors of military or natural disasters are at risk of infection due to loss of public health services. Rickettsial infections typically are manifested by fever, rashes, & vasculitis. Which of the following best characterizes rickettsia?
options: No need for an arthropod vector
Serology isn't an important tool for diagnosis
questions.explanation: Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular organisms and cannot grow on cell-free enriched culture media; they require living host cells (cell culture, embryonated eggs, or animal inoculation), making this statement false. They do affect vascular endothelial cells, are obligate intracellular, rely heavily on serology for diagnosis, and use phospholipase as a key virulence factor to escape the phagosome, so the other statements are true.
questions.keyConcept: Rickettsiae cannot be cultured on cell-free media because they are obligate intracellular organisms.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Rickettsia organisms infect humans worldwide. All are obligate intracellular parasites & transmitted by an insect vector & share which of the following manifestations of disease?
questions.explanation: Recurrence of relapsing fever is caused by successive antigenic variation of the Borrelia surface proteins: each time the immune system clears one antigenic variant, a new variant emerges and causes another febrile relapse.
questions.keyConcept: Antigenic variation drives the repeated relapses characteristic of relapsing fever.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The characteristic rash seen in many rickettsial diseases is a direct result of:
options: An allergic reaction to the arthropod bite
Vasculitis caused by damage to endothelial cells
Deposition of immune complexes in the skin
questions.explanation: Despite differing vectors and specific target organs, the various rickettsial diseases (spotted fever group and typhus group) share the common clinical triad-like pattern of fever and rash, reflecting the organism's tropism for vascular endothelium.
questions.keyConcept: Fever and rash are the shared clinical hallmark across rickettsial diseases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the cause of recurrence of relapsing fever?
options: Appearance of new antibiotic resistant strain
Multiplication of the organism in the to blood
questions.explanation: Cellulitis of the hand following a cat bite is not a feature of Lyme disease at all (it instead suggests Pasteurella multocida infection from an animal bite) — this is the false statement. Lyme disease is genuinely transmitted by tick bite, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, produces a migratory rash (erythema migrans), and is treated with tetracyclines.
questions.keyConcept: Lyme disease is tick-transmitted with erythema migrans; cat-bite cellulitis is unrelated to it.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of following isn't true about Lyme disease?
options: Manifested by cellulitis of hand following a cat bite
It is caused by borrelia burgdorferi
questions.explanation: Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) are injected into host cells via a type III secretion system and act mainly to inhibit phagocytosis and disrupt cytokine signaling, allowing the bacterium to evade the innate immune response.
questions.keyConcept: Yops disable phagocytosis and cytokine signaling in host cells, a key immune evasion mechanism for Y. pestis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-yearold man has HIV/AIDS characterized by a low CD4 & a high viral load. Highly antiretroviral therapy (MAART) Initiated. Which one of the drugs inhibits integrase enzyme??
questions.explanation: AZT and DDI are nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, and indinavir is a protease inhibitor, so together this three-drug regimen inhibits reverse transcriptase and protease, the two key enzymatic steps of HIV replication.
questions.keyConcept: AZT, DDI, and indinavir together inhibit reverse transcriptase and protease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 41-year-old HIV-infected male refused antiretroviral therapy diagnosed with Pneumocystis infection. Which of the following likely describes the state of this
options: Is at elevated risk for encephalitis
Has a life expectancy of about 5 years
Probably has declining levels of plasma viremia
Probably has a CD4* T cell count 200 cells/mm
Is unlikely to develop opportunistic infections at this stage
questions.explanation: Macrophages and monocytes act as a major reservoir for HIV because of their long lifespan and ability to harbor virus without being rapidly killed, allowing them to disseminate infection throughout the body, including across the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Macrophages and monocytes are long-lived HIV reservoirs that help disseminate infection throughout the body.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A known HIV patient was diagnosed with Pneumocystis Jiroveci infection. Which of the following most likely describes the state of this patient?
options: He's in the acute stage of HIV infection
Has a life expectancy of about 10 years
questions.explanation: Healthcare workers caring for Ebola patients and mourners handling bodies at burial ceremonies are at especially high risk for person-to-person transmission because both involve close contact with infectious body fluids.
questions.keyConcept: Healthcare workers and those handling bodies at funerals are at highest risk for Ebola transmission.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following are the examples of the route through which HIV can be transmitted from one person to another, EXCEPT?
options: Unprotected sexual contact with an infected person
From infected mother to the fetus
Exposure to contaminated blood & blood products 107NERS /
questions.explanation: The main rationale for combination antiretroviral therapy is to prevent the emergence of drug-resistant HIV variants, since the virus's high mutation rate would otherwise quickly select for resistance against any single drug.
questions.keyConcept: Combination ART is used mainly to prevent resistance from HIV’s high mutation rate.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: End of acute stage of HIV infection characterized by ____ e
options: Low T cell count, high viral load
Normal T cell count, Sero-negative patient
Normal T cell count, Sero-positive patient
questions.explanation: The incubation period for Ebola virus disease is approximately 2 to 21 days, which is a key epidemiological fact used in contact tracing and quarantine planning.
questions.keyConcept: Ebola’s incubation period is approximately 2-21 days.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Epstein-Barr virus causes Burkitt's lymphoma as it:
options: produces toxic metabolites that induce cells transformation
incorporates of its genome with the host genome while it's latent in B cells
weakens the immune response against tumor cells
questions.explanation: The viral protease enzyme targeted by HIV protease inhibitors cleaves large Gag-Pol precursor polyproteins into the smaller, functional structural and enzymatic proteins needed for assembly of mature, infectious virions.
questions.keyConcept: HIV protease cleaves precursor polyproteins into functional proteins required for virion assembly.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: For post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after a needle stick injury from an HIV- positive patient, anti-HIV medications should be taken for a duration of:
questions.explanation: The window period is the interval after HIV infection during which the viral load is already high but antibodies have not yet become detectable; seroconversion refers to the point when antibodies do become detectable, so it does not describe this earlier antibody-negative interval.
questions.keyConcept: The window period is the pre-antibody interval of high viral load and negative serology after HIV infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HAART treatment of HIV inhibits which of the following processes in viral replication?
questions.explanation: HIV infection begins when the viral envelope glycoprotein gp120 binds to the CD4 receptor on the T helper cell surface, triggering a conformational change that allows subsequent coreceptor binding and gp41-mediated membrane fusion.
questions.keyConcept: HIV entry begins with gp120 binding to the CD4 receptor.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HIV Chemoprophylaxis determine by...
questions.explanation: The current standard initial HIV screening test is the combined antigen/antibody (Ag/Ab) assay, which detects both the p24 antigen and HIV antibodies, shortening the window period compared with antibody-only or antigen-only tests.
questions.keyConcept: Combined Ag/Ab testing is the current standard initial HIV screening test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HIV cellular binding involves interaction between which pair of the following molecules?
questions.explanation: HIV requires the CD4 receptor to infect cells, so CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, which lack CD4, are not directly infected by HIV, unlike CD4+ helper T cells, monocytes, and macrophages, which all express CD4 and are genuine HIV targets.
questions.keyConcept: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells lack the CD4 receptor and are not directly infected by HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HIV infection begins when ____ a
options: The virus attaches to CD4 receptor on T helper cell by GP41
The virus attaches to CXCR4 receptor on T helper cell by GP41
The virus attaches to CD4 receptor on T helper cell by GP120
The virus attaches to CCR5 receptor on T helper cell by GP120
The virus attaches to CD4 receptor on T helper cell by GP24
questions.explanation: HIV replication does not depend on a DNA polymerase step (it uses reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease), so DNA polymerase inhibitors have no effect on HIV replication, unlike fusion, integrase, protease, and reverse transcriptase inhibitors, which are all established classes of anti-HIV drugs.
questions.keyConcept: DNA polymerase inhibitors do not target any step of the HIV replication cycle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) often includes a protease inhibitor. What is the function of the viral protease enzyme?
options: It converts viral RNA into DNA
It integrates the viral DNA into the host genome
It cleaves viral precursor proteins into functional proteins for virion assembly
It facilitates the fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane
questions.explanation: The frequency and severity of opportunistic infections in HIV-infected patients rise sharply once the CD4+ T cell count falls below about 200 cells/mm3, the classic AIDS-defining threshold.
questions.keyConcept: A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 marks sharply increased opportunistic infection risk in HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Innocent bystanders is
options: Killing of infected TH cells by CTLs
killing of infected TH cells due to accumulation of viral particles
killing of uninfected TH cells due to lack of Costimulation
Killing of infected T cells due to distortion of regulatory genes
killing of uninfected TH cells due to adsorption of viral particles on its surface
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase, which converts the HIV RNA genome into DNA, is the defining enzyme central to retroviral replication and a key driver of HIV pathogenesis (and drug resistance through its error-prone activity), unlike DNA gyrase, DNA polymerase, or topoisomerase.
questions.keyConcept: Reverse transcriptase is the defining, pathogenesis-critical enzyme of HIV replication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Latent infections of lymphocytes by EBV can result in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Standard post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after a high-risk needle-stick exposure to HIV consists of a 28-day course of antiretroviral medication, started as soon as possible after exposure.
questions.keyConcept: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is given for a standard 28-day course.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Retroviruses cause malignant transformations as it
options: produce proteins that deactivate host regulatory genes
integrate its genome to host's DNA causing mutations in regulatory genes
cause chronic inflammatory reaction around infected cells
produce proteins that enhances cell division
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr virus was first identified in, and remains classically associated with, Burkitt's lymphoma, in which latently infected B cells are driven toward malignant transformation by viral latent gene products (it is also linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, but Adult T Cell lymphoma is caused by HTLV-1, not EBV).
questions.keyConcept: Burkitt’s lymphoma is the classic malignancy associated with latent EBV infection of B cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The frequency and severity of 50. opportunistic infections in HIV patients signincantly increase when the CD4 cell count falls below what threshold?
questions.explanation: Quantitative RT-PCR (plasma HIV RNA viral load) is the best test for monitoring response to antiretroviral therapy because successful treatment is defined by suppression of viral load, whereas CD4 count and antigen/antibody tests are used more for staging and diagnosis than for tracking therapeutic response.
questions.keyConcept: Viral load by quantitative RT-PCR is the key test for monitoring HIV treatment response.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The opportunistic infections in AIDS are mainly due to the loss of ____ due
options: cell mediated immunity "depends on T-Helper cells"
questions.explanation: HIV is not transmitted by mosquito bites because the virus does not replicate in mosquitoes and the blood volume transferred is too small; unprotected sexual contact, mother-to-fetus transmission, and contaminated blood/blood products are all genuine transmission routes.
questions.keyConcept: Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV, unlike sexual, vertical, and bloodborne routes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The period after HIV infection when antibodies are NOT yet detectable, despite a high viral load, is known as the:
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia in an untreated HIV-infected patient is an AIDS-defining illness that occurs classically when the CD4+ T cell count has fallen below about 200 cells/mm3, indicating advanced immunosuppression and continued risk (not reduced risk) of further opportunistic infections.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumocystis pneumonia indicates a CD4 count typically under 200 cells/mm3 in untreated HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What are the immune cells acting as major reservoir & helping in dissemination of HIV?
questions.explanation: Seroconversion (the appearance of detectable HIV antibodies) typically begins within about 1-4 weeks after infection, marking the transition from the pre-antibody window period into a detectable antibody response.
questions.keyConcept: HIV seroconversion typically occurs within a few weeks of infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the importance of using combined therapy in HIV infection?
options: To avoid development of resistance to high mutation rate of HIV.
To have a combined effect on two different steps of HIV replication
To decrease the dose of each drug if taken alone
To decrease the duration of drug taking as combined drugs have a stronger effect.
To increased plasma half- life of absorbed dose of each drug
questions.explanation: Decisions about chemoprophylaxis against opportunistic infections in HIV-infected patients are classically guided by the CD4+ cell count, since specific CD4 thresholds (e.g., below 200 cells/mm3) define the risk for infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia.
questions.keyConcept: CD4+ cell count is the classic parameter guiding opportunistic infection chemoprophylaxis decisions in HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the initial screening test of HIV?
options: Detection of HIV Abs by ELISA test
questions.explanation: HIV's viral protease enzyme cleaves the Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors into individual functional proteins required for virion maturation, distinct from reverse transcriptase (RNA to DNA), integrase (DNA integration), or host enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Viral protease cleaves HIV precursor polyproteins into mature structural and enzymatic proteins.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the mode of action of indinavir uses as a part of highly active antiretroviral combination therapy HIV infection?
options: Is effective against HIV-1-I but not HIV-2
Seldom gives rise to resistant mutants HIV
Degrades the CD4 receptor on cells
Interferes with virus interaction with coreceptor
questions.explanation: Azidothymidine (AZT/zidovudine) is the prototype nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used against HIV; acyclovir and idoxuridine target herpesvirus DNA polymerase, ribavirin is used for RSV/hepatitis C, and oseltamivir targets influenza neuraminidase.
questions.keyConcept: AZT (zidovudine) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor used to treat HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: When does sero-conversion usually occur in HIV infected patient?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids are not a standard component of HIV treatment and can even be immunosuppressive; antiviral drugs, antibiotics for opportunistic infections, and immunotherapy approaches are genuine parts of HIV management.
questions.keyConcept: Corticosteroids are not part of standard HIV treatment regimens.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-viral drugs Is a reverse transcriptase inhibitor?
questions.explanation: AIDS-defining opportunistic infections arise mainly from the progressive loss of cell-mediated immunity, since HIV selectively depletes CD4+ T-helper cells that coordinate this arm of the immune response.
questions.keyConcept: Depletion of CD4+ T-helper cells cripples cell-mediated immunity, driving AIDS-related opportunistic infections.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following cells isn't infected by HIV?
questions.explanation: As acute HIV infection resolves and the patient enters clinical latency, the CD4 count partially recovers toward near-normal levels and the patient becomes seropositive as antibodies develop, distinguishing this stage from the high-viral-load, CD4-depleted peak of acute infection.
questions.keyConcept: The transition out of acute HIV infection is marked by CD4 recovery toward normal and seroconversion to antibody-positive status.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can't affect replication of HIV?
questions.explanation: gp120 is the HIV envelope glycoprotein responsible for initial binding to CD4 and then to a chemokine coreceptor (CXCR4 or CCR5) on the host cell surface; membrane fusion itself is mediated by gp41, and gp120 is highly variable (not conserved) and does elicit (though not fully protective) neutralizing antibodies.
questions.keyConcept: gp120 mediates receptor and coreceptor binding, while gp41 mediates membrane fusion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme required for viral replication plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of HIV infection?
questions.explanation: The envelope glycoproteins gp120 and gp41 on the outer membrane of HIV are essential for receptor/coreceptor binding and membrane fusion during cell entry, not polysaccharides, plain proteins, or lipopolysaccharides (a bacterial component).
questions.keyConcept: HIV envelope glycoproteins (gp120/gp41) mediate viral entry into host cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an important molecule present in the outer membrane of the HIV that helps to enter the cell?
questions.explanation: HAART regimens combine drugs that inhibit reverse transcriptase and protease, the two key viral enzymes required for reverse transcription of viral RNA and for cleavage of precursor proteins during virion maturation.
questions.keyConcept: HAART classically combines reverse transcriptase and protease inhibitors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about GP120?
options: Is highly conserved among different HIV variants
Binds to the viral coreceptor on the cell surface
questions.explanation: CD4 is the primary host cell receptor that HIV's gp120 envelope glycoprotein binds to on T lymphocytes; CD8 and CD3 are unrelated T cell surface markers, and gp120/gp41 are viral (not host) molecules.
questions.keyConcept: CD4 is the primary HIV receptor on T helper lymphocytes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following proteins/ glycoproteins isn't present in HIV?
options: A protein that increase expression of MHC class I
An enzyme that cleaves capsid polyproteins
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection that classically occurs once the CD4+ T cell count falls below about 200 cells/mm3, indicating advanced immunosuppression, not the acute stage or a low viral load.
questions.keyConcept: Pneumocystis pneumonia signals advanced HIV disease with CD4 counts typically below 200 cells/mm3.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: A 33 years old patient has fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy & pancytopenia. What is your diagnosis of this parasitic disease?
questions.explanation: Fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia together form the classic presentation of visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar), distinguishing it from toxoplasmosis, P. falciparum infection, babesiosis, or filariasis.
questions.keyConcept: The fever + hepatosplenomegaly + lymphadenopathy + pancytopenia tetrad is classic for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: An Indian patient has irregular fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy & pancytopenia. What is the drug choice in treatment of this parasitic disease?
questions.explanation: Pentostam (sodium stibogluconate), a pentavalent antimonial, is the classic first-line drug for treating Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), which is suggested by this patient's irregular fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia.
questions.keyConcept: Pentostam is the classic first-line treatment for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Animal inoculation is used in diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Animal inoculation (e.g., hamster inoculation) is classically used to diagnose Leishmania infection by detecting amastigotes in the spleen or liver of the inoculated animal, unlike Loa loa or Onchocerca volvulus, which are diagnosed by microfilariae in blood or skin snips.
questions.keyConcept: Animal inoculation is a diagnostic method specific to Leishmania, not filarial worms.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Diagnostic stage in tissue biopsy in Kala azar disease is:
questions.explanation: The amastigote is the diagnostic stage of Leishmania found within macrophages in tissue biopsy specimens (bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node) in Kala-azar.
questions.keyConcept: Amastigotes are the tissue-biopsy diagnostic stage of Leishmania in kala-azar.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Diagnostie stage in culture in Kala azar disease is:
questions.explanation: The promastigote is the diagnostic stage of Leishmania seen in culture (e.g., NNN medium) or within the sandfly, whereas the amastigote is the diagnostic stage seen in tissue biopsy.
questions.keyConcept: Promastigotes are the culture-diagnostic stage of Leishmania; amastigotes are for tissue.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Differential diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis:
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis presents with fever, wasting, and hepatosplenomegaly that overlaps with malaria, African and American trypanosomiasis, and schistosomiasis, making 'all of the above' the most complete differential diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: Visceral leishmaniasis has a broad differential including malaria, trypanosomiasis, and schistosomiasis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: A pregnant female had delivered a dead baby with enlargement of his head. The mother of this baby had history of contact with cats. What is yourdiagnosis?
questions.explanation: A dead baby with an enlarged head (hydrocephalus) born to a mother with a history of cat contact is a classic presentation of congenital toxoplasmosis, acquired transplacentally from a mother with primary Toxoplasma infection.
questions.keyConcept: Hydrocephalus in a stillbirth with maternal cat contact points to congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: A pregnant female had delivered a decid baby with microcephaly. The mother of this baby had history of contact with cats. Serological tests of this mother will show all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In a mother who has just had a congenitally infected baby (indicating acute primary infection during pregnancy), serology shows elevated IgM, IgA, and IgE along with a rising/elevated IgG level, but LOW (not elevated) IgG avidity, since avidity only rises months later as infection becomes chronic.
questions.keyConcept: Low, not elevated, IgG avidity is expected in the mother during acute toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Acute Toxoplasma infection is diagnosed by:
options: Positive Ig M and Ig A
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** All of the above. B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity.
questions.keyConcept: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies and mediate humoral immunity; for “Acute Toxoplasma infection is diagnosed by”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Acute toxoplasmosis is diagnosed by the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: High IgG avidity indicates a chronic, past Toxoplasma infection, not an acute one; acute toxoplasmosis is instead characterized by low IgG avidity along with elevated IgM, rising IgG titers, elevated IgA, and elevated IgE.
questions.keyConcept: High IgG avidity signals chronic, not acute, toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Cat is the main host for Toxoplasma gondii parasite because:
options: It has the sexual cycle inside it
It has the asexual cycle inside it
It passes mature oocyst in stool
It passes immature eggs in stool
questions.explanation: The cat is the definitive/main host for Toxoplasma gondii because the parasite's sexual cycle (gametogony, culminating in oocyst formation) occurs exclusively within the feline intestinal epithelium; cats pass immature (unsporulated) oocysts in stool, which then sporulate in the environment.
questions.keyConcept: The sexual cycle of Toxoplasma occurs only in the cat, making it the definitive host.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Chorioretinitis is caused by:
questions.explanation: Chorioretinitis is a classic ocular finding caused by Toxoplasma gondii, seen in both congenital and reactivated/acquired toxoplasmosis.
questions.keyConcept: Chorioretinitis is a hallmark ocular manifestation of toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Living Ag is used in which of the following tests?
questions.explanation: The Sabin-Feldman dye test uses live Toxoplasma tachyzoites as antigen; in the presence of complement and specific antibody, the live organisms lyse and fail to take up methylene blue dye, distinguishing it from tests that use fixed/killed antigen.
questions.keyConcept: The Sabin-Feldman dye test is unique in using live Toxoplasma tachyzoites as antigen.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Man can be infected with Toxoplasma by ingestion of:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** All of the above. Cats are definitive hosts of Toxoplasma gondii and shed oocysts; tissue cysts in meat are another important source of infection.
questions.keyConcept: Cats are definitive hosts of Toxoplasma gondii and shed oocysts; tissue cysts in meat are another important source of infection; for “Man can be infected with Toxoplasma by ingestion of”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Mature oocyst of Toxoplasma gondii
questions.explanation: The mature Toxoplasma gondii oocyst is disporocystic and tetrasporozoic, containing 2 sporocysts with 4 sporozoites in each.
questions.keyConcept: A mature Toxoplasma oocyst has 2 sporocysts, each with 4 sporozoites.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Neonatal jaundice occurs with:
questions.explanation: Neonatal jaundice is a recognized clinical feature of congenital toxoplasmosis, resulting from hepatic involvement (hepatitis) in the infected neonate, unlike the listed Leishmania and Trypanosoma species.
questions.keyConcept: Neonatal jaundice from hepatic involvement occurs in congenital toxoplasmosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Oocyst of Toxoplasma is found in:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Faeces of infected cat. Cats are definitive hosts of Toxoplasma gondii and shed oocysts; tissue cysts in meat are another important source of infection.
questions.keyConcept: Cats are definitive hosts of Toxoplasma gondii and shed oocysts; tissue cysts in meat are another important source of infection; for “Oocyst of Toxoplasma is found in”, the defining choice is “Faeces of infected cat”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Parasitophorus vacuole is present infection with which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites reside and replicate within a parasitophorous vacuole inside the host cell, a hallmark of its intracellular life cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Toxoplasma resides intracellularly within a parasitophorous vacuole.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Persistence of IgG antibodies against toxoplasma after 6 months from born from infected mother indicate
options: not a marker of newborn infection
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** Congenital infection. IgG and C3b are major opsonins that enhance phagocyte recognition and ingestion.
questions.keyConcept: IgG and C3b are major opsonins that enhance phagocyte recognition and ingestion; for “Persistence of IgG antibodies against toxoplasma after 6 months from born from infected mother indicate”, the defining choice is “Congenital infection”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Regarding toxoplasmosis in humans the true statements:
options: Infection could be transmitted from mother to fetus
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** All of the above. Separate parasites by host, vector, infective stage, diagnostic stage, and characteristic clinical manifestation. Applied to “Regarding toxoplasmosis in humans the true statements”: the discriminating answer is “All of the above”.
questions.keyConcept: Separate parasites by host, vector, infective stage, diagnostic stage, and characteristic clinical manifestation; for “Regarding toxoplasmosis in humans the true statements”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The infective stage of Toxoplasmosis
questions.explanation: The mature (sporulated), infective Toxoplasma gondii oocyst is disporocystic and tetrasporozoic — it contains 2 sporocysts, each holding 4 sporozoites (8 sporozoites total).
questions.keyConcept: The infective Toxoplasma oocyst contains 2 sporocysts with 4 sporozoites each.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The typical triad of congenital toxoplasmosis include:
questions.explanation: The classic congenital toxoplasmosis triad-related findings include hydrocephalus (or microcephaly), chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications; among the listed findings, hydrocephalus/microcephaly and intracerebral calcification are all part of the recognized syndrome, best captured by 'all the above.'
questions.keyConcept: Hydrocephalus/microcephaly and intracerebral calcification are both part of the congenital toxoplasmosis syndrome.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Toxoplasmosis should be excluded in the following condition:
questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** All of the above. Separate parasites by host, vector, infective stage, diagnostic stage, and characteristic clinical manifestation. Applied to “Toxoplasmosis should be excluded in the following condition”: the discriminating answer is “All of the above”.
questions.keyConcept: Separate parasites by host, vector, infective stage, diagnostic stage, and characteristic clinical manifestation; for “Toxoplasmosis should be excluded in the following condition”, the defining choice is “All of the above”.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Trans-placental infection occurs in:
questions.explanation: Transplacental (trans-placental) infection is a hallmark transmission route of Toxoplasma gondii, producing congenital toxoplasmosis in the fetus when the mother acquires primary infection during pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Transplacental transmission is characteristic of Toxoplasma gondii, causing congenital infection.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: What is the main cause of severe toxoplasmosis in HIV patients?
options: Transfusion with blood containing immature cyst
questions.explanation: Severe toxoplasmosis (toxoplasmic encephalitis) in HIV/AIDS patients is mainly caused by reactivation of latent tissue cysts (bradyzoites) as cell-mediated immunity declines, rather than by new acute infection.
questions.keyConcept: Reactivation of latent Toxoplasma tissue cysts drives severe disease in HIV patients.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding congenital toxoplasmosis?
options: Severity of fetal damage is maximum in 3d trimester
Chorioretinitis occurs if affection occurs in the 1 trimester
Occurs if the mother acquires primary infection during pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis specifically occurs when the mother acquires a primary Toxoplasma infection during pregnancy, allowing transplacental transmission; fetal damage is actually most severe with 1st-trimester infection, and most congenitally infected infants are asymptomatic at birth rather than usually symptomatic.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital toxoplasmosis requires primary maternal infection acquired during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Which of the following tests can be used to diagnose acute toxoplasmosis in HIV patients?
questions.explanation: In HIV/immunocompromised patients, antibody-based tests can be unreliable due to blunted immune responses, so direct detection methods — antigen detection and PCR — are preferred for diagnosing acute toxoplasmosis.
questions.keyConcept: Antigen detection and PCR are preferred over antibody tests for diagnosing acute toxoplasmosis in HIV patients.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: A female patient 50 years old living in West Africa complained of swelling in the back of her neck & irregular febrile attacks. By clinical examination she had generalized enlargement of lymph nodes & hepatosplenomegaly. This patient infected with 0...e
questions.explanation: Platelet dense (delta) granules store small molecules -- ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin -- involved in vasoconstriction and recruiting further platelets, whereas fibrinogen and other adhesive/growth-factor proteins are stored in the separate alpha granules, not the delta granules.
questions.keyConcept: Delta (dense) granules store small molecules like ADP/ATP/serotonin; fibrinogen instead resides in alpha granules.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: A patient has intermittent high fever & hepatosplenomegaly, enlarged posterior cervical lymph node & sleep disturbance. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin III, protein C, and heparin (endogenously, heparin-like heparan sulfate on endothelium) are all genuine physiological anticoagulant mechanisms that normally prevent intravascular coagulation. Fibrinogen, in contrast, is the procoagulant substrate converted to fibrin during clot formation -- it promotes, rather than prevents, coagulation.
questions.keyConcept: Fibrinogen is a procoagulant substrate, not one of the physiological mechanisms that prevent intravascular coagulation.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Acute Chagas disease is treated by:
questions.explanation: Acute Chagas' disease is treated with Benznidazole or Nifurtimox, the two standard trypanocidal drugs, rather than antimalarial, antileishmanial, or African-trypanosomiasis regimens.
questions.keyConcept: Benznidazole and Nifurtimox are the standard treatments for acute Chagas’ disease.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: All about Trypanosoma brucel gambiense is true EXCEPT:
options: It causes more lymphatic affection than T. rhodesiense
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is an anthroponotic (not zoonotic) parasite, with humans as the main reservoir; T. b. rhodesiense is the zoonotic form maintained in wild game animals and cattle. It does occur in West Africa, causes prominent lymphatic involvement, is transmitted by Glossina palpalis, and its infective stage is the metacyclic trypomastigote.
questions.keyConcept: T. b. gambiense is anthroponotic (human-maintained), unlike the zoonotic T. b. rhodesiense.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: All about Trypanosoma brucel rhodesiense is true EXCEPT:
options: It causes more lymphatic affection than gambiense
questions.explanation: Margination describes neutrophils adhering to the vessel wall near an inflamed area (via selectin/integrin interactions), the first step before diapedesis (squeezing through the endothelium) and chemotaxis (migration to the infection site).
questions.keyConcept: Margination is neutrophil adherence to the capillary wall, the first step of extravasation toward infection.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: All about Trypanosoma cruzi is true EXCEPT:
options: It occurs in Central & South America
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi is a stercorarian parasite, transmitted via triatomine bug faeces deposited on the skin, not a salivarian parasite transmitted through an insect bite/saliva as with the African trypanosomes; it does occur in Central & South America, is zoonotic, is transmitted by Triatoma, and its infective stage is the metacyclic trypomastigote.
questions.keyConcept: T. cruzi is stercorarian (faecal transmission), not salivarian, unlike the African trypanosomes.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Animal inoculation is used to detect posterior nucleated form of:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils constitute the first line of cellular defense against acute bacterial infection, arriving within hours via chemotaxis and phagocytosing invading bacteria, before monocyte/macrophage recruitment provides sustained, longer-term defense.
questions.keyConcept: Neutrophils are recruited first (within hours) to acute bacterial infection, ahead of monocytes/macrophages.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Antigenie variation is present in:
questions.explanation: Antigenic variation (variant surface glycoprotein switching) is a defining immune-evasion mechanism of Trypanosoma brucei, allowing successive waves of parasitemia; it is not a feature relied upon by Trypanosoma cruzi or Plasmodium malariae in the same way.
questions.keyConcept: Antigenic variation via VSG switching is characteristic of Trypanosoma brucei specifically.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Armadillo is the reservoir host of:
questions.explanation: B and T lymphocytes together constitute the lymphocyte population, which mediates adaptive (specific) immunity -- B cells for humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity and T cells for cell-mediated immunity -- distinguishing lymphocytes from the innate phagocytic/granulocytic cell types (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes).
questions.keyConcept: Lymphocytes (B and T cells) are the WBC class responsible for adaptive, antigen-specific immunity.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Cardies muscle is especially affected the following disease:
questions.explanation: Chagas' disease (American trypanosomiasis, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi) especially affects cardiac muscle, producing chagasic cardiomyopathy, unlike Plasmodium species which do not preferentially target the heart.
questions.keyConcept: Chagas’ disease classically causes cardiac muscle damage (chagasic cardiomyopathy).

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Cardiomegaly is one of the manifestation of:
questions.explanation: Humoral immunity defends against bacteria mainly through antibody-mediated mechanisms -- opsonizing bacteria for phagocytosis, activating the complement system, and activating certain WBCs via antibody-dependent mechanisms -- but the actual engulfing (phagocytosis) of bacteria is carried out by phagocytic cells themselves, which is a cellular, not humoral, action.
questions.keyConcept: Direct engulfment of bacteria is a cellular phagocytic action, not itself a humoral immune mechanism.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Chagas's disease is caused by:
questions.explanation: Thrombin activates the fibrinolytic system indirectly by promoting endothelial release of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and by binding thrombomodulin to activate protein C, helping balance clot formation with its own eventual breakdown -- a key feedback control on coagulation.
questions.keyConcept: Thrombin has a dual role: driving clot formation while also triggering feedback mechanisms (via thrombomodulin/protein C and tPA release) that limit clot extension.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Chancre is more severe in:
questions.explanation: Intravenous heparin is the appropriate immediate treatment for a hypercoagulable (pro-thrombotic) state, since it rapidly potentiates antithrombin III to inhibit thrombin and factor Xa, halting further clot propagation -- unlike sodium citrate (an anticoagulant only in vitro), vitamin K agonists (which would promote clotting), or bed rest alone (which does not treat the underlying hypercoagulability).
questions.keyConcept: IV heparin rapidly inhibits thrombin/factor Xa via antithrombin III, making it first-line for acute hypercoagulable states.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Chancre is the cutaneous manifestation of?
questions.explanation: A trypanosomal chancre can occur at the tsetse fly bite site in both forms of African sleeping sickness, caused by the polymorphic trypanosomes Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense.
questions.keyConcept: The trypanosomal chancre can occur in either gambiense or rhodesiense sleeping sickness.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Chancre is the primary lesion found in:
questions.explanation: A chancre (trypanosomal chancre) is the primary inflammatory skin lesion that forms at the tsetse fly bite site in African sleeping sickness, distinguishing it from Kala azar, malaria, Chagas' disease (chagoma), and filariasis, none of which produce this specific lesion.
questions.keyConcept: A chancre at the bite site is the classic primary lesion of African trypanosomiasis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Constipation due to megacolon & difficulty of swelling due to megaoesophagus may occurs in infection with ____
questions.explanation: Non-specific (innate) immunity is rapid, includes both cellular (phagocytes, NK cells) and humoral (complement, interferons) components, and interferons are indeed proteins released by virus-infected cells to limit viral spread -- but innate immunity does not generate immunological memory (memory cells), which is a hallmark of adaptive (specific) immunity instead.
questions.keyConcept: Innate immunity lacks immunological memory (memory cells), unlike adaptive immunity.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Early stages of sleeping sickness is best treated by:
questions.explanation: B-lymphocytes mediate humoral immunity by differentiating into antibody-secreting plasma cells upon antigen recognition, distinguishing their function from T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and the granulocytic/phagocytic white cell lines.
questions.keyConcept: B-lymphocytes are the WBC class responsible for humoral (antibody-based) immunity.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Hepatosplenomegaly occurs in infection with:
questions.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly can occur with malarial infections (P. falciparum, P. vivax), Chagas' disease, and African trypanosomiasis (polymorphic trypanosoma), making 'all of the above' the most complete answer.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatosplenomegaly is a shared feature across malaria, Chagas’ disease, and African trypanosomiasis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Romana sign is a manifestation of:
questions.explanation: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments (not nucleated cells) derived from megakaryocytes; they are not actively phagocytic, and severe thrombocytopenia (low platelet number, not a 'thrombocytopathy') causes bleeding/purpura. Their aggregation, however, is genuinely stimulated by ADP and thromboxane A2 released from activated platelets in a positive-feedback loop, recruiting further platelets to the growing plug.
questions.keyConcept: ADP and thromboxane A2 released from activated platelets amplify aggregation via positive feedback.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Romana sign is:
options: Enlarged lymph nodes in posterior triangle of the neck.
questions.explanation: Romaña's sign is unilateral periorbital (palpebral) edema that develops at the site of conjunctival inoculation with Trypanosoma cruzi in acute Chagas' disease.
questions.keyConcept: Romaña’s sign is unilateral periorbital edema from ocular inoculation with T. cruzi.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The anthroponotic type of trypanosomes is:
questions.explanation: B-lymphocytes are the white blood cell type that differentiates into antibody-secreting plasma cells, mediating humoral immunity -- distinguishing them from T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity), macrophages and neutrophils (phagocytosis), and basophils (mediator release).
questions.keyConcept: B-lymphocytes uniquely differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The diagnostic stage of Trypanosoma brucei is:
questions.explanation: The diagnostic stage of Trypanosoma brucei found in blood and CSF is the polymorphic trypomastigote, reflecting the pleomorphic (slender and stumpy) forms characteristic of African trypanosomes.
questions.keyConcept: The polymorphic (pleomorphic) trypomastigote is the diagnostic blood/CSF stage of T. brucei.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The diagnostic stage of Trypanosoma cruzi in acute stage is:
questions.explanation: Helper T-lymphocytes (CD4+) assist B-lymphocytes in mounting an effective antibody response by providing cytokine signals and co-stimulation needed for B-cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
questions.keyConcept: Helper T-lymphocytes provide the cytokine/co-stimulatory signals that enable B-lymphocytes to produce antibodies.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The diagnostic stage of Trypanosoma cruzi in lymph node or muscles is:
questions.explanation: In tissues such as lymph node or muscle, Trypanosoma cruzi exists intracellularly as the amastigote form; the trypomastigote form is instead the diagnostic stage found circulating in peripheral blood.
questions.keyConcept: T. cruzi’s tissue (intracellular) diagnostic stage is the amastigote; trypomastigotes are the blood stage.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The infective stage of trypanosomes is:
questions.explanation: Diapedesis is the active squeezing of white blood cells between endothelial cell junctions to exit the blood vessel into the surrounding tissue, occurring after margination (adherence to the vessel wall) and before chemotactic migration toward the infection site.
questions.keyConcept: Diapedesis is the physical passage of WBCs through the vessel wall, following margination.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The metacyclic trypomastigote form of Trypanosoma cruzi are found in:
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi's infective metacyclic trypomastigotes develop in the hindgut of the triatomine (reduviid) bug and are passed in its feces, unlike African trypanosomes which develop in the tsetse fly's salivary glands/mouthparts.
questions.keyConcept: T. cruzi’s infective stage develops in the vector’s hindgut and is transmitted via feces, not saliva.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The organisms develop in the hind gut of the vector & the infective stage with the faeces of the insects occurs in infection with ____
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi (the monomorphic trypanosome) develops in the hindgut of the triatomine bug vector, and its infective metacyclic trypomastigote stage is passed in the insect's faeces — a stercorarian transmission pattern distinct from the salivarian transmission of the polymorphic African trypanosomes.
questions.keyConcept: Hindgut development and faecal transmission of the infective stage is characteristic of T. cruzi (monomorphic trypanosome).

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The parasitic form found in affected tissues during chronic Chagas disease is:
questions.explanation: Chemotaxis is the directed migration of white blood cells toward a site of infection or inflammation, guided by a concentration gradient of chemical signals (e.g., complement fragments, bacterial products, cytokines) -- occurring after the cell has already marginated and undergone diapedesis out of the vessel.
questions.keyConcept: Chemotaxis is chemical-gradient-directed WBC migration toward infection, the final step after margination and diapedesis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The vector of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is:
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (West African sleeping sickness) is transmitted by the riverine tsetse fly, Glossina palpalis, in contrast to T. b. rhodesiense, which is transmitted by the savannah tsetse fly Glossina morsitans.
questions.keyConcept: Glossina palpalis is the vector for T. b. gambiense (West African sleeping sickness).

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The vector of Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense is:
questions.explanation: Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (East African sleeping sickness) is transmitted by the savannah tsetse fly, Glossina morsitans, in contrast to the riverine Glossina palpalis, which transmits T. b. gambiense.
questions.keyConcept: Glossina morsitans is the vector for T. b. rhodesiense (East African sleeping sickness).

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The vector of Trypanosoma cruzi is:
questions.explanation: Severe bone marrow depression (e.g., from radiation, drugs, or aplasia) suppresses production of all blood cell lines -- red cells, white cells, and platelets -- together, producing pancytopenia/aplastic anemia, rather than isolated changes in a single cell line or increased coagulability.
questions.keyConcept: Severe marrow depression produces aplastic anemia via pancytopenia (suppression of all cell lines), not an isolated defect.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: The wrong statement about Glossina palpalis is:
options: Both sexes feed on blood of vertebrates
questions.explanation: Glossina palpalis (tsetse fly) transmits Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, not Trypanosoma cruzi, which is instead transmitted by triatomine (reduviid) bugs; both sexes of Glossina palpalis do feed on vertebrate blood and are daytime feeders as blood-dependent (though not permanently attached) flies.
questions.keyConcept: Glossina palpalis transmits T. b. gambiense, never T. cruzi, which requires a triatomine vector.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true about Rhodesian sleeping sickness?
options: Has an acute course of disease
questions.explanation: Marked Winterbottom's sign (enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes) is characteristic of the chronic Gambian form of sleeping sickness, not the acute Rhodesian form, which progresses to CNS involvement before prominent lymphadenopathy develops. Rhodesian sleeping sickness is indeed caused by Glossina morsitans, has an acute course, and is a zoonosis.
questions.keyConcept: Marked Winterbottom’s sign is a Gambian, not Rhodesian, sleeping sickness feature.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Winterbottom's sign is more severe
questions.explanation: Incompatible blood transfusion triggers an acute hemolytic reaction: destroyed red cells release hemoglobin (causing hemoglobinuria and later anemia), release intracellular potassium (raising, not decreasing, blood K+), release histamine (contributing to the reaction), and in neonates the resulting bilirubin load can cause kernicterus -- so the statement that K+ decreases is the false one, since hemolysis actually raises plasma K+.
questions.keyConcept: Hemolysis from incompatible transfusion raises (not decreases) plasma potassium, since intracellular K+ is released from destroyed RBCs.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.text: Xenodiagnosis is used for diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Opsonization coats bacteria with antibodies or complement fragments (e.g., C3b), which are recognized by specific receptors on neutrophils, greatly enhancing the efficiency of phagocytosis -- essentially making the bacteria "tasty" (more readily engulfed) to phagocytic cells.
questions.keyConcept: Opsonization (antibody/complement coating) enhances neutrophil recognition and phagocytosis of bacteria.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A blood film of a patient with chronic bacterial infection will most likely show an increase in:
questions.explanation: Prostacyclin (PGI2), released by healthy endothelium adjacent to an injury, inhibits platelet aggregation in that surrounding normal vessel wall, confining the platelet plug specifically to the site of injury and preventing it from spreading into uninjured vessel segments.
questions.keyConcept: Prostacyclin from adjacent healthy endothelium confines platelet plug formation to the injury site.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A blood film of a patient with viral infection will most likely show increased:
questions.explanation: A platelet count of 200,000/mm3 falls within the normal adult reference range of roughly 150,000-400,000/mm3, whereas the other listed values (80,000, 800,000, and 130,000, depending on the exact reference range used) fall outside or at the border of the normal range.
questions.keyConcept: A platelet count of 200,000/mm3 lies comfortably within the normal 150,000-400,000/mm3 reference range.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Azurophilic granules are present in:
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins (mainly albumin and globulins) help retain fluid within blood vessels via oncotic pressure, participate in blood clotting (fibrinogen and clotting factors), and bind/transport hormones and other substances -- but oxygen transport in blood is carried out by hemoglobin within red blood cells, not by plasma proteins.
questions.keyConcept: O2 transport is a red-cell hemoglobin function, not a role of plasma proteins, unlike oncotic pressure, clotting, or hormone transport.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: B lymphocytes can be discriminated from T lymphocytes by using:
questions.explanation: Plasmin, generated from plasminogen, is the key proteolytic enzyme that slowly digests and dissolves fibrin clots over time (fibrinolysis), gradually restoring normal blood flow through a previously clotted vessel as the vessel wall heals.
questions.keyConcept: Plasmin gradually dissolves fibrin clots via fibrinolysis, restoring vessel patency as healing occurs.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Basophils:
options: Their granules contain histamine and heparin
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B because basophil granules contain histamine and heparin and participate in immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Basophils are rare in blood, are not highly phagocytic, and do not have the classic multilobed neutrophil nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Heparin potentiates antithrombin and acts rapidly in vivo and in vitro; unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT; for “Basophils”, the defining choice is “Their granules contain histamine and heparin”.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: During granulopoiesis, specific granules start to appear in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B because the myelocyte stage is where lineage-specific granules become evident, allowing distinction between neutrophilic, eosinophilic, and basophilic lines. Promyelocytes mainly contain azurophilic primary granules.
questions.keyConcept: Identify the cell or tissue by its microscopic morphology, granules, and functional specialization; for “During granulopoiesis, specific granules start to appear in”, the defining choice is “Myelocytes”.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Monocytes can differentiate into:
questions.explanation: Plasminogen is converted to active plasmin by multiple activators, including activated factor XII, thrombin, and tissue factors released from injured tissue (tissue plasminogen activator, tPA) -- reflecting several convergent pathways that trigger fibrinolysis once a clot has served its purpose.
questions.keyConcept: Plasminogen activation to plasmin can be triggered by several convergent pathways: factor XII, thrombin, and tissue-derived activators.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Neutrophilic specific granules are characterized by containing:
options: They are the minority of granules

questions.explanation: **Why it is correct:** B & C. Heparin (and all heparin products) must be stopped; HIT is managed with a non-heparin anticoagulant. Argatroban (a direct thrombin inhibitor) and fondaparinux (a factor Xa inhibitor) are both appropriate choices, so the combination B & C is correct. Protamine sulfate (A) only reverses heparin’s anticoagulant effect and has no role in treating the immune thrombocytopenia itself.
questions.keyConcept: Heparin potentiates antithrombin and acts rapidly in vivo and in vitro; unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT; for “Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia can be managed by”, the defining choice is “B & C”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Warfarin is used for maintenance rather than initiation of DVT treatment because:
questions.explanation: HIV entry begins when the envelope glycoprotein GP120 binds the CD4 receptor on host T-helper cells; this binding induces a conformational change in GP120 that exposes a coreceptor-binding site (for CCR5 or CXCR4), after which GP41 mediates membrane fusion. The initial, defining cellular binding interaction is therefore between CD4 and GP120.
questions.keyConcept: HIV cell entry starts with CD4-GP120 binding, followed by coreceptor engagement and GP41-mediated membrane fusion.

Warfarin / reduces synthesis of II, VII, IX and X

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.explanation: LMWH offers predictable kinetics and lower HIT risk, but is not categorically more efficacious than UFH.
questions.keyConcept: Heparin potentiates antithrombin and acts rapidly in vivo and in vitro; unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT; for “Which is NOT an advantage of dalteparin over unfractionated heparin”, the defining choice is “Greater efficacy”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.keyConcept: Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor; idarucizumab is its specific reversal agent; for “Which is NOT an advantage of rivaroxaban or dabigatran over warfarin”, the defining choice is “No dose adjustment in renal failure”.

questions.explanation: Renal impairment increases rivaroxaban exposure and may require dose reduction or avoidance.

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.explanation: INR monitors warfarin, not dabigatran; dabigatran usually requires no routine coagulation monitoring.
questions.keyConcept: Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor; idarucizumab is its specific reversal agent; for “Which monitoring pair is wrongly matched”, the defining choice is “Dabigatran / INR”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is WRONG concerning protamine sulfate:
options: It is the proper antidote for heparin
Has slight anticoagulant effect with large dose

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which statement about dabigatran is incorrect?
options: Rapid onset and long duration up to six days
Absorption is reduced by proton-pump inhibitors
Potentially usable in selected liver dysfunction

questions.keyConcept: Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor; idarucizumab is its specific reversal agent; for “Which statement about dabigatran is incorrect”, the defining choice is “Rapid onset and long duration up to six days”.

questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K.
questions.keyConcept: Platelet-released ADP promotes recruitment and aggregation of additional platelets through positive feedback; for “Which statement about warfarin is most likely true”, the defining choice is “Inhibits vitamin K activation”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.keyConcept: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing functional factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S; for “Adverse effects of warfarin include all action of the following EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “Teratogenic effect”.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following antidotes are correctly matched EXCEPT:

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following drugs are oral anticoagulants EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis, Chagas disease (T. cruzi), African trypanosomiasis, and toxoplasmosis can all be transmitted via contaminated blood transfusion because their infective forms circulate in donor blood. Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae, while present in blood, are not known to establish infection through transfusion, since transmission normally requires the mosquito intermediate host stage.
questions.keyConcept: W. bancrofti is not transmitted by blood transfusion, unlike Leishmania, T. cruzi, African trypanosomes, or Toxoplasma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following increase the warfarin EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae are sheathed (loosely, not tightly -- the sheath is a thin, often barely visible membrane), show nocturnal periodicity in peripheral blood, and have a tapering posterior end and rounded anterior end both devoid of nuclei -- describing the sheath as 'tight' is the incorrect statement, since W. bancrofti's sheath is characteristically loose/thin, unlike some other sheathed microfilariae.
questions.keyConcept: W. bancrofti's sheath is loose and thin, not tight, distinguishing it from other microfilarial species.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following statements are true about warfarin EXCEPT:
options: It is highly bound to plasma protein
Can cross placenta & is secreted in milk
Inhibits synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania donovani, African trypanosomes, and Trypanosoma cruzi can all cross the placenta and cause congenital (transplacental) infection of the fetus. Wuchereria bancrofti does not cross the placenta to cause congenital filariasis in the classic sense.
questions.keyConcept: Congenital (transplacental) transmission is recognized for Toxoplasma, Leishmania, and trypanosomes, but not for W. bancrofti.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: As regards anticoagulation in pregnancy all the following are EXCEPT:

LMWH is preferred to heparin as induces less osteoporosis
Warfarin is preferred to heparin in first trimester

questions.keyConcept: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing functional factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S; for “As regards anticoagulation in pregnancy all the following are EXCEPT”, the defining choice is “LMWH is preferred to heparin as induces less osteoporosis”.
